The Gemelli, located in the north-west of the Italian capital, is renowned for treating reigning popes. Pope John Paul II stayed there so many times that the Vatican worked with the hospital to establish a high-security papal suite.

The Chilean-American author Isabel Allende has won Spain’s €1m (£843,000) Premio Planeta, one of the world’s most lucrative literary prizes, under a pseudonym, with a sequel to her celebrated debut novel, The House of the Spirits.

Allende, 84, won the 75th edition of the award on Thursday with La hora antes del alba, which returns to the characters of her 1982 novel, a multigenerational family saga set against political upheaval in a country inspired by Chile.

The new story follows Alba, the granddaughter of Esteban Trueba and Clara del Valle, as she tries to recover from imprisonment and torture during Pinochet’s dictatorship, according to Reuters. Allende said the book would bring the universe of The House of the Spirits to a close. The 1982 novel is often read alongside Daughter of Fortune and Portrait in Sepia as part of a loose trilogy of interconnected family sagas.
Speaking at the award ceremony in Barcelona, attended by King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia, Allende said it was “like winning the Nobel”.
“I had never entered a competition because I wanted to avoid the embarrassment of coming last,” she said. “At my age, there is very little to lose.”

She said she had been prompted to write the sequel by decades of readers asking what happened to Alba. She also drew parallels between the political circumstances surrounding the novel and the contemporary rise of extremism. Allende was forced into exile after the 1973 military coup led by Augusto Pinochet that overthrew the Chilean president Salvador Allende, a cousin of her father. Allende had been Latin America’s first democratically elected Marxist leader. Under Pinochet’s regime, an estimated 40,000 people were tortured and more than 3,000 killed.
“Now that I see so many democracies threatened by authoritarianism, extreme nationalism and even fascism, I feel again the fear that led me to leave my country,” she said.

Allende is one of the best-known writers in the Spanish-speaking world, whose books have sold more than 80m copies worldwide and been translated into more than 40 languages. The prize is open to unpublished manuscripts, with the option of submitting under a pseudonym, and Allende entered under the name Luz Ventura, with the fictional title Los que faltan.

However, the judges may have been able to pick up on Allende’s style. “I’d be very surprised if the judges did not know that it was Isabel Allende,” said Prof Duncan Wheeler, the chair of Spanish studies at Leeds University and president-elect of the Association of Hispanists of Great Britain and Ireland. “You have to bear in mind that the Planeta prize is one of the most generously remunerated in the Spanish-speaking world, but definitely not the most prestigious.”

The prize has at times faced criticism over the choice of winner. In 2021, the prize was awarded to La bestia, a thriller published under the pseudonym Carmen Mola, which had been marketed as the identity of a female author. At the awards ceremony, it was revealed that Mola was in fact three male writers – Jorge Díaz, Agustín Martínez and Antonio Mercero.

The prize is run by Planeta, one of the largest publishing groups in the Spanish-speaking world, and includes the condition that the winning book be published by them. Allende has been published by Plaza & Janés, an imprint of Penguin Random House, since The House of the Spirits, so this marks a significant coup for Planeta.

Despite the option to submit pseudonymously, the prize has a history of favouring established writers and TV figures: past winners of the prize have included prominent Spanish-language authors such as Juan Marsé and Manuel Vázquez Montalbán, and the controversial TV personality Juan de Val.

Asked about the perceived trend of awarding the prize to figures known for appearing on TV shows, José Creuheras, the president of the Planeta Group, said, according to the Spanish newspaper El País: “I’m not in a position to say whether the Planeta Prize has more or less prestige than it did in the past. We have some of contemporary literature’s biggest names among our winners and finalists. The prize’s reach, as measured by the figures, speaks for itself, and the number of people taking an interest in the Planeta is growing.”
The runner-up was the Spanish writer and screenwriter Sergio Hernández, whose historical novel La añoranza won €200,000.
When it comes to oysters, Andrew Zimmern believes location is everything.

The celebrity chef and television personality, who will host the Oyster Bash at the New York City Wine & Food Festival on Saturday, said the secret to a great oyster lies in its flavor, texture and, perhaps most importantly, where it originates.
"Oysters really taste of place," Zimmern told Fox News Digital.

Much like wine grapes, oysters develop distinctive characteristics based on their environment. Water conditions, food sources and even the composition of the seafloor can influence their flavor and appearance.
Zimmern has experienced these differences firsthand, tasting oysters harvested just a few hundred yards apart that delivered dramatically different flavors.
"One's very sweet, one's very saline. And it really depends on what you like," he said.
As for his own preferences, Zimmern gravitates toward oysters with a particular combination of flavors.
"I like oysters that are coppery, taste like a cross between pennies and celery and have enough salinity to sort of carry the oyster," he said.

He's particularly fond of West Coast oysters, although he noted that East Coast growers are increasingly producing oysters with similar flavor profiles by carefully selecting growing locations based on the food available in the water.
But while oyster aficionados might debate which region produces the best shellfish, Zimmern is decidedly less particular about how they're prepared.
Raw, grilled, fried or baked, he's game for all of them.
"If the oyster is flavorful enough, you can do anything with it," he said.

Zimmern recalled visiting an oyster restaurant outside Houston where the raw oysters were unremarkable, but the grilled preparations — including versions with spinach, cheese, garlic, butter and hot sauce — were extraordinary.
He also has a soft spot for fried oysters and regularly makes oyster chowder during the colder months.
"I love cooked oysters," he said. "I love oyster chowder. I make oyster chowder almost every other week in the wintertime."

The cast of "Little House on the Prairie" is opening up about the brutal reality of filming the hit TV series.
Cast members were guests on Patrick Labyorteaux's podcast to discuss their experiences on the show. He asked Alison Arngrim, who starred as Nellie Oleson, what the first day was like for her.
"Complete chaos and confusion," Arngrim admitted.

She explained that she hadn't known she was supposed to show up with her character's signature ringlet curls, "So it was lots of panic and phone calls back and forth, and then massive curling of my hair. So yeah, bananas. And then, first day on location, of course, I pass out."
"So, I was off to just a rousing start right there," she added.
The conversation also included fellow cast members Dean Butler, Pamela Roylance and Jennifer Donati, as well as Tracy and Victor French, the children of late cast member Victor French.
Labyorteaux also starred in "Little House on the Prairie" as Andy Garvey.

During a later conversation about how hot it was in Simi Valley, where the show was filmed, Arngrim joked that the cast and crew were able to tell when summer hit because the "first day of summer is when Alison hits the ground, because I was out like that. It was that hot."

Speaking again of her first day on set, she explained that she was "so disciplined," she approached the director and said, "Excuse me, I think I'm going to faint" before she "completely lost consciousness and dropped."

"It's like basically how to not pass out was the challenge," she continued. "It was insane, though – the great thing is that other people began to pass out, so people realized it wasn't me, the first one being Sean Penn."
Penn, who was a child at the time, "didn't wake up and come back to work. That was it, he was done for the day."
Arngrim said, "That's when they decided maybe it was not just me, that it was actually that hot."

Later in the podcast, the subject of their least favorite episodes came up, and Arngrim shared that she disliked any episodes where sporting events were involved, because that meant sitting in bleachers "where it was 100 million degrees" for hours at a time while crew members filmed reaction shots.

She recalled one of these shoots when Charlotte Stewart, who played school teacher Eva Beadle Simms, "was just sitting there, and she had in fact lost consciousness and fainted and blacked out, but just didn't fall over, and they didn't know she was out."

About the sweltering set, Butler admitted, "You just had to do whatever strategy you could. I always felt sorry for the women on the set … [the men] were basically dressed in a shirt and pants and dog-eared boots" while the female cast members wore dresses, petticoats, stockings and sometimes wigs.

Roylance shared that Michael Landon, who acted as executive producer, writer and director on "Little House" in addition to his starring role, let her film one scene with her blouse unbuttoned and her sleeves rolled up because "it was just miserable hot" that day on the set.
"It kind of just wasn't done," she admitted about the way she wore the blouse, "but it's in the shot, you can see it in the episode, and I was so grateful for that."
She also said that Stan Ivar, who played her husband, gave her "a little fan that I wrapped around my leg and blew up my skirt."

Donati, who, along with her twin sister, was an infant when she played Baby Rose Wilder, joked, "I don't want to brag, but I think I was the most pampered cast member there. They didn't let me get hot."

"Little House on the Prairie" was a Western family drama loosely based on Laura Ingalls Wilder's semi-autobiographical books. It follows the Ingalls family as they build a life in Walnut Grove, Minnesota, during the late 19th century.

Landon starred as the Ingalls family patriarch, Charles, Karen Grassle played his wife, Caroline, and Gilbert portrayed their daughter, Laura. The series premiered on NBC in 1974 and ran for nine seasons, through 1983, followed by three television movies.
Pope Leo XIV leaves hospital days after lung cancer surgery

Pope Leo XIV left Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Saturday afternoon and returned to the Vatican after doctors said he was well enough to be discharged following surgery that removed part of his right lung.

The Vatican press office released a statement outlining details from Dr. Luigi Carbone,the Pope's personal physician, and Professor Stefano Margaritora, Gemelli's chief of thoracic surgery who led the team that operated on Leo. The two doctors said the pope had undergone blood tests and a chest X-ray that morning, with the results confirming his clinical condition meant he could leave hospital.

They said he was expected to lead the Angelus prayer from the window of the papal apartment on Sunday.Video showed Leo waving to well-wishers outside the hospital as he walked out without physical support, flanked by officials and security guards in dark suits.
Before leaving, the pope had celebrated Mass in a room set aside for that purpose on the hospital's 10th floor, according to the press office.

Vatican spokesperson Matteo Bruni said "the estimated post-operative recovery time will be about one week." Leo's discharge came on his fifth day in hospital and was sooner than had been expected at the time of the operation's announcement.
Leo, 71, had told crowds in St. Peter's Square last Sunday that doctors had discovered a "localized nodule" in his lung at a "very early stage."
"Following their advice, I have therefore decided to undergo an operation to remove it," he said.

The surgery on Tuesday went further than the nodule, however, with surgeons using a video-assisted technique to remove the lower lobe of the pope's right lung in an operation that lasted about 90 minutes. His doctors said lung tissue examined afterward confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma. With adenocarcinoma making up about 40% of all lung cancers in the U.S., it is the nation's most common form of lung cancer, according to the Lung Cancer Foundation of America.
That is true among nonsmokers too, according to Dr. Otis Brawley, an oncologist at Johns Hopkins University and former chief medical and scientific officer of the American Cancer Society.

Leo is not known to have smoked, but cancer does run in his family. His mother, Mildred, died of cancer in 1990, and on Tuesday the Vatican announced that his older brother Louis, who lives in Florida, has been hospitalized with a form of cancer.
Doctors not involved in the pope's care say the treatment so far points to a cancer that has been caught early.

"The fact that surgery was the first tool that they utilized is a really good sign," Dr. Vin Gupta, a pulmonologist and board member of the American Lung Association, told NPR. "It suggests that they think this is early stage."

Gupta said the fact that doctors removed a larger portion of the lung than first announced is not in itself a bad sign. "People have parts of their lungs removed all the time for all sorts of reasons, and they recover just fine," he said. "And in his case, he's pretty robust at baseline from a health standpoint."
Leo still exercises regularly, playing tennis each week with his personal secretary and riding horses at Castel Gandolfo, the papal retreat to the south of Rome.
The Vatican has not announced any further treatment.

Leo's office has cleared his public schedule until at least Oct. 20. His next major international trip, set for early November, includes Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, where he lived on and off for two decades and holds citizenship.

"He had a minimally invasive surgery," said Dr. Jonathan Villena Vargas, a cardiothoracic surgeon at Weill Cornell Medical Center in New York City. "Because we do this all the time, most patients are allowed to travel about two weeks after the surgery."

Brawley from Johns Hopkins agreed. "I think he can do it," he said, adding that patients in good physical shape who have this type of procedure "very frequently are back to normal in seven to 10 days."
Zelenskyy urges support for new US sanctions on Russia after Trump puts them on hold

KYIV, Ukraine — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged supporters Saturday to speak out in defense of new U.S. sanctions against Russia, hours after President Donald Trump signed an executive order pausing a sweeping package of restrictions targeting the Russian economy.
The White House decision has further raised fears that Ukraine could be left exposed to Moscow's escalating assaults with winter approaching.

Russian attacks overnight killed at least four people, including an ambulance driver, and wounded dozens, officials said. Ukrainian drones killed a woman in a Russian border region and disrupted flights at Moscow's airports, according to Russian authorities.

In a statement on social media, Zelenskyy described Trump's move to put sanctions on hold as unfortunate, but did not directly criticize the U.S. leader despite deepening tensions between Ukraine and Washington in recent days.

"A decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end," Zelenskyy wrote.

Later, in audio clips answering journalists' questions, Zelenskyy thanked Democrats and Republicans who backed the legislation and praised its bipartisan support. He said blocking it would encourage Russia to continue killing and do nothing to bring the war to an end.
He also added that limiting Ukraine's ability to retaliate against Russian attacks would not bring peace.

"Nevertheless, we very much hope — and I personally hope — that the president of the United States of America will do everything possible to make Putin stop the killing, stop the attacks on our energy infrastructure, and end this war," he said.
Critics say Trump's decision helps Putin

Named after late South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling Russia's 4 1/2-year-old war against Ukraine. The bill had sought to sanction Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving.
Trump personally signed the legislation just last month and his move came just two days before a deadline set in the law itself for its implementation.
The president told Congress that the pause was in the national interest but gave no further details.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who co-drafted the bill, said in a statement that Trump was turning his back on "the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, and our European allies."
"These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin," Blumenthal said.

Trump's unexpected decision comes a week after he stunningly said the U.S. had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine in its war with Russia.
Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter."

The decision has been pilloried by Republicans and Democrats alike who say it will help Russia execute its war against Ukraine — without making a difference to global fuel prices, which are elevated mostly due to Trump's war on Iran.
Kyiv says Moscow carried out a 'massive' energy strike
Zelenskyy also said Saturday that Moscow had carried out a massive strike on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, targeting more than 15 sites across the country.
"The sheer scale and unrelenting pace of Russia's strikes, specifically against our energy sector, are unfortunately having severe consequences," he said.
Ukraine's air force said that Russian forces launched four cruise missiles and 332 attack drones overnight. All of the missiles and 289 of the drones had been suppressed or destroyed, it said.

Russia's heavy bombardment of the power grid ahead of winter has been an annual feature of the war, aimed at wearing down Ukraine's appetite for the fight by denying civilians heat and running water. Ukrainian officials have warned that Russia is stockpiling ballistic missiles for more attacks in the coming months.

Russian attacks killed three people in the Ukrainian city of Sloviansk, Vadym Liakh, head of the city military administration, said Saturday. Writing on social media, Liakh said that two apartment blocks were partially destroyed and other homes damaged.

A Russian strike also killed an ambulance driver in Ukraine's Kherson region, head of the local military administration Yaroslav Shanko said. The strike, which used guided bombs, wounded at least 33 others, he said.
Ukrainian drones kill 1, ground hundreds of flights at Moscow airports
Elsewhere, a Russian woman was killed in a Ukrainian drone attack in the Russian border region of Belgorod, local officials said.

Russia's Ministry of Defense said Saturday that its forces had shot down 610 Ukrainian drones overnight over 15 Russian regions, as well as the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that more than 100 drones were shot down en route to the Russian capital. More than 350 flights were canceled or delayed at Moscow's airports, local media reported, as planes were grounded in response to incoming drones.
The Kremlin announced Saturday that Russian President Vladimir Putin had approved a government program to help restore trade and logistics facilities damaged in drone attacks.
Decades after apartheid, South Africans seek justice for crimes of the past
SHARPEVILLE, South Africa – Paulina Mathinye gestures with anguish at the rows of garbage-strewn graves, overrun with weeds, in the cemetery where her father is buried.

"Look at that, where they sleep," she says of the dozens of Black protesters buried here, all of whom were killed when police opened fire on March 21, 1960 in what became one of the bloodiest days in apartheid history.
"Why are they dirty? It's a disgrace," says the 71-year-old grandmother, who wears a floral dress and a smart sunhat.

The cemetery, like much else in this visibly poor township about an hour's drive from Johannesburg, has been left to decay. But Mathinye notes that for one day a year at least, when South Africa's political elite descend to commemorate the massacre, the graveyard is spotless. The anniversary is a public holiday known as Human Rights Day.
"I'm still angry. My anger comes out because that's the day my father was shot," says Mathinye, who was just five years old at the time.
She says her father's part in what became a turning point in the struggle against apartheid has not been sufficiently recognized by the current democratic government.
And she says she wants justice – however delayed.
That's why she's signed up to take part in a potential class action lawsuit 66 years later, along with Sharpeville survivors and the families of Sharpeville victims.
At least 69 people were shot by police that day. They had been demonstrating against the country's pass laws – which restricted black people's movements and where they could live and work.
While it's unclear if any perpetrators are still alive, those taking part in the case hope it could lead to reparations.

But first, the group's lawyers must challenge an apartheid-era law that continues to block their efforts to seek legal redress. The law remains in force decades after apartheid ended and a Black-majority government took power.

In September they filed an application in the Gauteng High Court challenging the continued existence of the Indemnity Act 61 of 1961. If the court finds the law unconstitutional, and also certifies a class action for survivors and dependants of those killed, then claims for individual damages could follow.
Mathinye says the repercussions of that day in 1960 have affected her whole life.
Without her father, the main breadwinner, she couldn't finish school. That, in turn, affected the lives of her children and grandchildren.
"So we struggled a lot. And we are still struggling now, because nothing has been happening," she told NPR.
If the case goes ahead and succeeds, Mathinye says she'll use any money from reparations to fix up her modest home and pay for her four grandkids' educations.
The Sharpeville case is just one in a new wave of legal efforts that are seeking truth, accountability and reparations for apartheid-era crimes before it's too late.

"It's crucial that these issues of deep injustice are properly dealt with and that South Africa confronts them and does not sweep them under the carpet," says Daniel Leader, an international human rights lawyer advising the South African legal team representing the Sharpeville survivors and families.
Other cases include a court ruling last year that found South Africa's first Nobel Peace Prize laureate, Chief Albert Luthuli, was beaten to death by apartheid police in 1967.

Luthuli, the former leader of the African National Congress — Nelson Mandela's party — had previously been ruled to have died after being struck by a train. The new ruling overturned the finding of an earlier inquest.

The inquest into the 1985 killings of four anti-apartheid activists known as the "Cradock Four" has also been reopened. The activists were abducted and killed by apartheid security forces near the Eastern Cape town of Cradock. Although the officers involved are all dead, the victims' families hope the inquest will establish who ordered the killings.
And the inquest into the torture and death of Steve Biko, the iconic Black Consciousness leader who died in police detention in 1977, has also returned to court.

"It's very clear that the murder of Steve Biko was exactly that, murder," Biko's son Nkosinathi told media in September at the reopened inquest. "We hope that this inquest will eventually get to this very certain, unambiguous finding."
The original inquest in 1977 heard from members of the security branch who said Biko had fallen and hit his head in a "scuffle with security police."

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC), a court-like restorative justice body set up in the 1990s to uncover the truth about human rights violations during apartheid, re-examined the Biko case.
It denied amnesty to security officers who testified, saying they hadn't been truthful. That essentially cleared the way for possible prosecutions, but they never happened.

In fact, hundreds of the TRC's recommendations for prosecutions were delayed or never pursued. Last year, President Cyril Ramaphosa established a formal inquiry to investigate whether the recommendations were deliberately shelved.

The inquiry is looking into whether there was a secret deal between the old leaders of the apartheid regime and the country's new Black leaders not to prosecute cases in the interests of reconciliation. Its findings are due in December.
Back at the Sharpeville cemetery, Paulina Mathinye and three other descendants of those killed in the massacre, pause in front of a memorial plaque before exiting the graveyard.
Vincent Thamae, from the NGO, Voices of Sharpeville which works with survivors and descendants asks that they take leave of the dead.
"We ask of those who are sleeping here to be with us as we pursue justice for them," he says.
Pedro Neto’s double condemned Everton to a first defeat of the season as Chelsea won 2-0 at the Hill Dickinson Stadium despite the loss of goalkeeper Emi Martinez to a head injury.
Neto opened the scoring inside the first minute of the second half on Saturday and secured the three points during the 11 added minutes following the lengthy treatment given to the stricken Martinez.
The Argentinian international was involved in a sickening head clash with Everton defender Jarrad Branthwaite and was taken to hospital.
“As far as I know he left the stadium conscious. Right now he’s in the hospital doing the precautionary tests, so let’s see,” said Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso.
A first away win of the season lifts Chelsea above the Toffees into the top four and the Blues also recorded a first clean sheet in 23 Premier League games.
“We needed one of these wins away. We have played very professional, very serious, looking solid. It is a very good win,” added Alonso.
“We need to get many more clean sheets for the rest of the league games but for sure the first one of the season feels good and now we need to keep going this way.”
After a slow start, a fiery-tempered encounter sparked into life when Everton midfielder Harrison Armstrong launched into a tackle on Josh Acheampong for the first of five first-half yellow cards.
That challenge also enlivened the home crowd and spurred Everton on to their best spell of the game.
Thierno Barry was guilty of another wasteful day in front of goal as the Frenchman planted a header from Jack Grealish’s cross too close to Martinez.
Chelsea have made a habit of fast starts under Alonso, but it took until four minutes before half-time to threaten when Moises Caicedo blasted off the bar from a well-worked corner.
Everton were furious that Morgan Rogers escaped a second booking just before the break after a thunderous clash with England teammate James Garner.
That proved to be a huge decision as the visitors this time flew out of the blocks at the start of the second period.
Jorrel Hato got to the byline and his low cross fell to Neto, who had time to control before firing low past Jordan Pickford.
Chelsea had not kept a Premier League clean sheet since January, but were rarely troubled by an Everton side short on forward options, despite the loss of Martinez.
“I just felt that Chelsea had that little bit more flair and ability which we didn’t possess at the right moments today,” said Everton boss David Moyes.
The treatment for Martinez threatened to halt Chelsea’s momentum as they controlled the second half.
Belgian Mike Penders replaced the Chelsea number one for his first Premier League appearance but had little to do bar dealing with a few desperate Everton crosses.
At the other end Pickford made a fine save to deny Joao Pedro.
But Chelsea did get their second goal when Neto coolly stroked into the bottom corner after Jordan Henderson’s free-kick was blocked by the Everton wall.
“We are really pleased. Shame for Emi but we wish you all the best. This win is for him,” Neto told TNT Sports after his first Premier League brace.
“We need a clean sheet, to be honest. I think we did a very good game. Emi deserved this, Mike did as well.”

Lawyers for Democratic United States Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota have demanded the return of property seized in a federal raid of her Washington, DC home, accusing the US Department of Justice of conducting a politically motivated investigation and failing to follow judicial instructions during the search.

“The political motivations behind this pre-election investigation and search are clear as day,” Omar’s lawyers wrote in a letter sent to federal prosecutors on Friday and obtained by The Associated Press news agency. “This search was neither justified nor lawful.”

In the letter, Omar’s lawyers, Amy Jeffress and Joshua Matz, challenged an investigation into her immigration history, saying there was “no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status”.
The letter accuses federal agents of threatening the separation of powers and failing to comply with a magistrate judge’s instructions for the search of Omar’s northeast Washington home on Monday.

Federal agents searched Omar’s home on Monday as part of an investigation into alleged immigration fraud. Authorities seized her phone and passport, and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, according to The Washington Post. Her lawyers also asked authorities to preserve audio and video recordings from the search.

Omar’s lawyers claim that investigators did not provide a copy of the warrant to them in advance, nor did they contact the House of Representatives’ Office of General Counsel, which disregarded the magistrate judge’s orders. The notice would have allowed Omar to seek legal counsel and potentially leverage legislation that could have challenged the warrant.

Her lawyers said the procedures outlined by the judge are intended to protect Omar’s constitutional rights as a sitting member of Congress, and safeguard against the seizure of materials related to her legislative work.
Her lawyers also argued that the investigation was politically motivated due to its proximity to the November midterm elections.

“Historically, the Department has refrained from this type of investigative activity so close to an election, so as to avoid even the appearance of politically motivated law enforcement actions,” they wrote.
The Justice Department rejected the accusations, describing the letter as “riddled with false allegations and inaccuracies”.
“Our attorneys and law enforcement partners complied with all court orders and legal obligations, as they always do,” Justice Department spokesperson Emily Covington said.

Omar became a naturalised US citizen in 2000 after fleeing Somalia with her family as a child, according to her House biography. She has repeatedly rejected allegations by conservative critics about her immigration status, which was also probed in 2019 during Trump’s first administration.

Omar’s lawyers have requested records relating to the 2019 inquiry into her immigration history. The former investigation found insufficient evidence of wrongdoing to warrant a full investigation, according to The Washington Post.
The scope of the current investigation remains unclear.

The search took place days after Trump attacked Omar at a rally in Tennessee, describing her home country as a place of “crime and squalor” and suggesting that Vice President JD Vance and others were investigating her. Hours after the search, Trump denied any involvement, telling reporters the matter was “really up to the DOJ”.
Thousands of Tunisians have marched through the capital to protest against President Kais Saied, worsening living conditions and restrictions on political freedoms.
The latest demonstration in Tunis on Saturday was led by the Tunisian General Labour Union (UGTT), an influential trade union federation, alongside opposition parties and civil society organisations.
It was the largest protest against Saied in years, bringing together political opponents whose longstanding divisions have weakened their ability to challenge his rule.
The AFP news agency reported that more than 3,000 people were on the march, but the total could not be independently confirmed.
Protesters gathered along Habib Bourguiba Avenue, a major street in central Tunis, as hundreds of police deployed across the capital. Several surrounding roads were closed.

The crowd included lawyers, doctors, journalists and the unemployed, as well as activists and members of parties from across the political spectrum. They demanded the release of detained government critics and an end to restrictions on trade union rights.
Placards reading “No democracy without freedoms” and “No dignity with poverty” reflected the political and economic grievances driving the demonstration.
Protesters also revived a slogan demanding the government’s removal, widely heard during Tunisia’s 2011 uprising.
Addressing the rally on Saturday, UGTT leader Salah Eddine Salmi criticised the concentration of political power in the presidency and said “silence will no longer be acceptable”.
The political demands came alongside mounting frustration over the cost of basic goods and declining purchasing power.
Tunisia has struggled with prolonged economic difficulties, deteriorating public services, recurring water and electricity cuts, as well as shortages of medicines and other essentials.
Demonstrator Yassine Gharseli, who travelled from Sfax, about 250km south of Tunis, said repeated disruptions to basic services had deepened his frustration with the authorities.
“I came from Sfax to stand up for my freedom,” he told the Reuters news agency at the demo, expressing his determination to continue speaking out.
Saturday’s march followed other demonstrations over similar grievances.
On August 20 , protesters in Tunis rallied against rising prices and shortages of basic goods.
Last month, fuel transport workers went on a two-day strike over wages and working conditions, led by a union federation affiliated with the UGTT.
The demands recall the uprising that ousted longtime President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali in 2011, which helped ignite protests across the Arab world.
Tunisia subsequently held competitive elections and expanded political freedoms, but unemployment and struggling public services remain persistent sources of anger.

Saied came to power promising an alternative to that political system; however, in 2021, he suspended parliament and dismissed the government, saying he was confronting corruption and political deadlock.
He later dissolved parliament and a new constitution increased presidential powers in 2022.

In a dark underground hideout, dim light spills from a handful of oil lamps. A comrade fiddles with a rifle. A red flag hangs on one of the roughly hewn stone walls, bearing a hammer and sickle on a white star — the symbol of the ChineseWorkers' and Peasants' Red Army. Weapons are scattered on the ground. One is picked up, and soon the action moves into the snowy forest, where gunfire erupts among the trees.

Such a scene could fit in a new installment of "Call of Duty," the popular first-person shooter game that transports players to battlefields past, present, and future. But it is actually from "The Defiant." The game is currently being developed by the Chinese studio Hoothanes Technology in Hangzhou. It tells the story of Chinese forces fending off the Japanese army in the 1930s and 1940s.

Developer Connor Xu tells DW the weapons featured in the game are unique. They were used only in Asia and are therefore unfamiliar to many Western players, he says. The same goes for the story, which Xu says has never before been told in a video game.

"The Defiant" is also designed to appeal to an international audience. In just a few years, China has emerged as a major player in the global gaming industry despite strict regulations, censorship and a former ban on video game consoles.
Gaming is part of everyday life in China

More than 700 million people in China regularly play video games. According to market research company Newzoo, most consider gaming an important part of their lives. Many use games to stay in touch with friends.

"Games make life more interesting," developer Xu says. "I can try different roles, different stories, different characters, because we only have one life to live, but we can play a role in another story. That's really attractive, I think, to Chinese users."

People in China primarily play games on PCs and smartphones, while consoles are much less common. There are historical reasons for that: While gamers in Europe and North America debated whether PlayStation or Xbox was the better console in the early 2000s, the devices were not officially sold in China between 2000 and 2014. Chinese authorities said the restrictions were intended to protect children and teenagers from becoming addicted to gaming.
Limits on gaming time and extensive controls

Minors in China are currently allowed to play online games for no more than three hours a week. There are no such limits for adults, but gaming is subject to strict controls. Anyone who wants to play must register using their real name and a personal identification number. That effectively allows the state to track who plays what and when, as well as whom they communicate with.

There is also a gray area that the Chinese government appears to tolerate. Some players log in using VPNs, giving them access to games that are not officially available in China. Some younger players use their parents' accounts to get around the limits on gaming time.

Despite its strict controls on underage gamers, China has become increasingly receptive to video games in general, having recognized the industry's enormous economic potential. Early on, games released for Chinese players often appeared to be copies of Western titles. At the same time, Chinese tech companies such as Tencent and NetEase invested in numerous Western gaming companies.

One distinctive feature of the Chinese market is its licensing system. "Unlike a lot of the other big video games markets in the world, China has a tightly regulated and licensed official video games market," George E. Osborn tells DW. The journalist advises NGOs and governments on video games and spoke at the Gamescom congress. In his book "Power Play," he describes how authoritarian states use video games to pursue political objectives.

The rule for all games in China is simple: No license, no sales. "That system essentially forces developers who want to release their video games to go through multiple layers of approval from China's Ministry of Propaganda, Ministry of Culture," Osborn says.

Games are prohibited from containing material that threatens China's unity, sovereignty or territorial integrity, among other restrictions. Pornographic content and gambling are also banned. Games may not incite crimes that threaten national security or spread information authorities believe could disrupt public order.

"The whole point around this criteria is that it's deliberately designed to be pretty vague," Osborn says. Whether a game violates the rules is a matter of interpretation. Sometimes games are altered even after release. In the 2025 action role-playing game "Wuchang: Fallen Feathers," for example, enemies based on famous Chinese figures from the Ming Dynasty suddenly could no longer be killed. Instead, they would collapse from exhaustion.

The Chinese action role-playing game "Black Myth: Wukong" became an unexpected international hit in 2024. By then, it was clear Chinese developers could do more than cater to the domestic market — they could create successful games for a global audience as well. The game was inspired by the 16th-century Chinese literary classic "Journey to the West."

Osborn sees nothing wrong with bringing Chinese culture to audiences around the world. The question, he says, is how much the state actually intervenes in the games themselves. "I think in general, video game players are actually quite deeply skeptical of these kinds of things. They are generally very good at spotting when someone might be selling to them or someone might be propagandizing. And so I think if it's too obvious, it won't work," he says.

Because of the licensing system, Western developers also have to comply with government requirements if they want to sell their games in China. And they do want to, Osborn says, because the market is too big to ignore. "But I think when you start thinking about the potential impact this has on creative standards around the world, I think it's really important that developers ask themselves the question of what will we or won't we compromise on here?"

He fears the real danger lies in self-censorship. That could lead developers, for example, to leave queer characters out of their games. That would represent a major step backward, he says, because games help many people explore their identities.

China is not the only country where games are modified to comply with national regulations. In Germany, for example, symbols that violate the country's constitution, such as the swastika, may not be shown in games unless the game in question explicitly contributes to the country's culture of remembrance. Depictions of extreme violence also have to be removed from German versions.

Glorifying violence is prohibited in China, too, yet Xu's team is still allowed to develop a war game. How does this add up? Xu explains it this way: "I think in this game, the most important thing is not violence. The most important thing is to tell history."
Xu says the team is committed to delivering a historically accurate product. Whether it succeeds will be for historians to judge.

The cemetery in the West Bank village of Al Mughayyir is dotted with burial sites draped with the Palestinian flag, marking the graves of local men and boys killed in clashes over the years with Israeli settlers and Israeli security forces.
It was one of the places 17-year-old Omar Nassan insisted that CBC News visit back in April.

Both now lay in that small cemetery overlooking hills, fields and a busy roadway.
Omar and Aws had been good friends, and he talked about life in Al Mughayyir with a deep sense of frustration and fatalism.

"To be honest, I didn’t tell this to anyone … but I already accepted death. I’m going to be dead," Omar said. "I lost my friend and he’s not the first first friend I lose, whether it’s getting killed or in prison. He’s not the first or the last friend I lose, so I already accept death. I’m going to be next."
Omar said many young men in the village felt the same way. The stress of life in the Occupied West Bank, combined with the constant threat of violence, had worn them down.
"It can’t get more dangerous," he said. "We’re used to that now. It’s our life."
Omar’s words on that April afternoon proved tragically prescient.

Omar’s mother, Rania, says her son loved to eat, did well at school and had a natural talent for working with computers. Omar learned English, she says, at school in her native country, Egypt.

The Nassan family believes Omar was shot by an IDF sniper soon after he left his home. The IDF won’t confirm that.

As for the shooting at the school in April, the IDF says the case is currently under review by the Military Advocate General’s Corps, but won’t say whether the review or its ruling will be made public.

Pope Leo XIV was discharged from the hospital on Saturday after undergoing surgery to remove a cancerous nodule from his right lung.

The pontiff, who had been recovering at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital since Tuesday, walked out unaided before spending a couple of minutes speaking with well-wishers. He appeared to accept a gift of a homemade smiling Pope figure before getting in a car and being driven back to the Vatican.

“Following the conclusions reached by the medical team this morning, Pope Leo XIV will be discharged today from Gemelli Polyclinic Hospital, where he was admitted for surgery on his right lung,” the Holy See Press said Saturday in a statement, before the Leo left the building mid-afternoon.
He is expected to recite the Angelus prayer from the window of the papal apartment at St. Peter’s Basilica on Sunday, according to the statement.

The pontiff’s personal doctor, Dr. Luigi Carbone, and the head of thoracic surgery at Gemelli Hospital, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, said that in light of blood tests and a chest X-ray performed Saturday morning, and after an assessment of his clinical condition, “the Holy Father has been deemed fit for discharge from the hospital.”
So far, Leo’s doctors have given no indication that the pontiff might need any further treatment. And the Vatican has not indicated whether the cancer might have spread.
Leo, who is a Chicago native, resumed working from the hospital on Thursday, his doctors and the Vatican reported.

The Vatican on Friday released the first images of Leo since his surgery, showing him celebrating Mass inside the hospital, as doctors said that tests confirmed the “continued improvement” in his recovery.

The photos show Leo standing up at the altar in green vestments celebrating Mass in a makeshift chapel that has been set up for him. Spokesman Matteo Bruni said he presided alone over the liturgy, distributed Communion to medical personnel and Vatican gendarmes present and delivered a homily.
His discharge from the hospital comes less than a month before Leo is scheduled to jet off for a two-week trip to South America, which is set to start Nov. 11.
Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori, in an interview on Peruvian television, said the pace of the pope’s recovery could determine whether Leo makes his weeklong apostolic visit to Peru.
“I want the pope to know that here in Peru, millions of us are praying for his speedy recovery,” Fujimori said Wednesday.
Leo was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma, a type of non-small cell lung cancer, after doctors examined the nodule they had removed from his right lung.
Non-small cell lung cancer accounts for 80% of all cases of the disease, according to the American Lung Association.
This type of cancer affects both smokers and nonsmokers, although Leo is not known to ever have been a smoker.

The initial lump was detected during a routine check, the Vatican has said. The leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics took the rare step of revealing the health issue — the first of his papacy — during his Sunday noon prayer last week.
Leo waved to crowds outside Rome’s Gemelli Hospital as he entered Tuesday.
The procedure was led by Dr. Stefano Margaritora, Gemelli’s chief thoracic surgeon, with medical staff reciting the rosary prayer in the hospital chapel as the operation began.

EDMONTON, Alberta — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney made a final appeal to voters considering a path toward independence in his home province of Alberta on Friday, warning that a referendum is a dangerous gamble at a time of growing threats to Canada’s sovereignty.

With U.S. President Donald Trump waging a trade war and threatening to make Canada the 51st state, Carney warned that the referendum comes at the “worst possible time” and urged Albertans not to take the outcome for granted.
“Don’t let anyone tell you this is already decided. Turnout will determine the outcome,” Carney told a pro-Canada rally in Edmonton, where he grew up.
“This is not a game. This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians,” he said.

Monday’s vote is not a direct referendum on independence. Alberta, home to most of Canada’s proven oil reserves — the fourth largest in the world — will decide whether to remain a province or instruct the government to begin the legal process toward a future referendum on separation.

Carney’s closing appeal came after two days of campaigning against separation in the province. Earlier Friday, the Liberal prime minister joined Alberta’s conservative premier Danielle Smith in a show of unity against independence.
Smith praised Carney for improving relations with a province that frequently clashed with his predecessor, Justin Trudeau, over his carbon tax and other energy policies.
“I think what we can agree on is that we have had some real change in the last 18 months,” Smith said alongside Carney in Red Deer, Alberta.
Smith noted that Carney grew up in Alberta and remains an Edmonton Oilers fan.
“He can’t be all bad, right?” she joked.
“Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us. Never. Never,” Carney warned Friday in Edmonton, repeating a warning he made a day earlier in Calgary.
At Thursday’s Calgary rally and Friday’s Edmonton rally, the crowd erupted in its loudest applause when Carney spoke about reducing Canada’s economic dependence on the United States.
Carney acknowledged Alberta’s longstanding resentment of federal energy policies.
“Growing up, I remember how Ottawa made Albertans feel like our resources weren’t our own,” he said.
But he also emphasized his deep ties to the province.
“Alberta is my home. I grew up here. This city, this province, this country have given me everything: my family, my education, my values,” he said.
Some Albertans say the vote shouldn’t have been called
Outside the Edmonton rally venue Friday, Alberta independence supporters waved flags and held a sign reading “Say no to Carney’s new world order.”
Smith called the referendum despite opposing independence herself. She recently cited a poll showing 22% of Albertans support separation, a figure she said was still too high.

Smith also faces pressure from separatists within her governing United Conservative Party. Former Premier Jason Kenney said the independence movement gained influence within the party as activists angry over COVID-19 restrictions, some influenced by conspiracy theories, embraced separatism.
But some Albertans who want to remain in Canada are angry with Smith for calling the vote.

“I think it’s a travesty really to be putting our province and our country through this when such a small portion of people are rabble rousing and saying they want to separate from Canada,” said Deb Lee, a retired Calgary resident who voted in advance to remain in Canada.
Smith said Carney had substantially addressed seven of nine federal laws Alberta opposed. She also cited cooperation on a proposed oil pipeline.
Independence advocate Tanya Clemens dismissed the agreements between Carney and Smith as “basically pinky promises” that came with too many conditions.
Political leaders unite against separation
Carney’s chief political rival, federal Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre, also urged Albertans Friday to remain in Canada.
“Don’t leave your fellow Canadians behind. Lock arms with them,” Poilievre said.

Despite their agreement on keeping Alberta in Canada, Carney and Smith remain divided over nine other questions on Monday’s ballot involving immigration and provincial powers. Smith wants voters to approve them, while Carney has urged their rejection.
“For the first time in a long time, Alberta and Canada are walking together,” Smith said.

Afghanistan faces record hunger levels amid rampant rights violations

Acute malnutrition and hunger in Afghanistan have reached the highest levels ever recorded, with 15.9 million people facing acute food insecurity and conditions set to worsen in the coming months, according to a global hunger monitor report released on Thursday.
UN agency heads are calling for emergency support to stem the crisis, as a separate report details serious human rights violations – from public floggings to a new ban on demonstrations.
- 15.9 million Afghans are facing acute food insecurity
- 3.4 million are experiencing emergency food insecurity conditions, which precedes famine, and conditions are expected to worsen
- New UN report on human rights in Afghanistan reveals serious violations, from public floggings to a fresh ban on demonstrations

Record acute malnutrition levels for the August–October period have seen hunger levels grow for millions of Afghans – according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), a global initiative aimed at informing decisions based on five phases of food security.

Economic pressures are straining households nationwide, contributing to more than 32 per cent of the population facing crisis-level acute food insecurity phase three or above, including 3.4 million people experiencing emergency phase four conditions.
The current deterioration is driven by disease outbreaks and inadequate water, sanitation and hygiene conditions, compounded by sharply reduced access to nutrition services, the report found.

The situation is expected to worsen from November to April during the winter lean season, when nearly 19.2 million people are projected to face phase three or above, including five million people in emergency food insecurity conditions.
Acute malnutrition is also set to grow significantly, with 4.04 million children under age five projected to need treatment between January and December 2027.
“Although improved rainfall and better agricultural production have supported food availability, declining humanitarian assistance is reducing households’ ability to cope,” the report warned.

The World Food Programme (WFP) and Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) issued a stark message on Thursday, calling for urgent funding to scale up food assistance, emergency agricultural support and malnutrition prevention and treatment.

“We still have a window to act, but it is closing fast,” WFP country director John Aylieff said. “With urgent support, families can get through the winter with dignity. Without it, many will face impossible choices no parent should have to make.”
FAO representative Richard Trenchard said families need opportunities to earn a dependable living that “helps them withstand the next shock” and support to get through this winter.

The UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) on Thursday reported the continued erosion of basic human rights across the country between July and September, with women and girls bearing the brunt of restrictions imposed by Taliban authorities.

Girls’ school ban: Girls remain barred from formal education beyond grade six. Asked about the ban, a Taliban spokesperson said that “problems and considerations” had to be taken into account from the perspective of Sharia law.

Women arrested, detained or cautioned: UNAMA documented more than 50 cases related to the hijab, mostly in Herat and Kabul. In one case, a 13-year-old girl was held overnight. Women were also blocked from entering health clinics and markets without a male guardian, or mahram.

Arbitrary arrests and detentions: The mission recorded at least 443 cases and 97 incidents of ill-treatment by virtue and vice inspectors over offences including hijab violations, trimmed beards, skipped prayers and listening to music.

Judicial corporal punishment: While the de facto Supreme Court stopped publicly announcing such cases on its social media account and website in April, UNAMA documented public lashings of 22 men and six women on charges including theft and adultery, and the arrest of 14 former security force members, with at least four others killed.

Media and civic freedom curtailed: Several outlets were suspended without clear reasons or appeal procedures. A journalist arrested in July 2025 remains in custody without conviction. A new police law, published in August, bans all demonstrations.

Cross-border violence: Since October 2025, 512 civilians have been killed and 1,236 injured, with 33 casualties in the latest quarter, including children killed in Pakistani airstrikes on homes in Kunar and Helmand.

On Oct. 17, 2016, Orbital ATK (now Northrop Grumman Space Systems) returned to flight, successfully launching a cargo shipment to the International Space Station (ISS) after its previous cargo mission failed to launch.

The private spaceflight company was contracted by NASA to fly cargo to the ISS, and stakes were high for this launch. Orbital ATK's last attempt nearly two years earlier ended in a catastrophic explosion a few seconds after liftoff.

Despite some delays, the newly upgraded Antares rocket flawlessly blasted off into the night sky from NASA's Wallops Flight Facility in Virginia. Six days later, the Cygnus cargo spacecraft arrived at the ISS to deliver food, supplies and science experiments to the crew.

For the International Space Station to be able to sustain a continuous human occupancy, periodic cargo deliveries are needed. Russia fulfills part of this requirement with its Progress spacecraft, and both ESA (European Space Agency) and JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) have contributed with their Automated Transfer Vehicle (ATV) and H-II Transfer Vehicle (HTV), respectively.

For its part, NASA contracted with Orbital (today, Northrop Grumman) and SpaceX to fly commercial resupply service missions. Both were needed to keep the U.S. operating segment of the station well supplied and with the science and research materials needed for the crew's work.

Though adjustments can be made to go without one or more of these vehicles for a short period of time, the Progress, Cygnus and Dragon are key components of the ISS's continuous operation. So returning a vehicle to flight after a catastrophic exploration is important to well-being of the International Space Station program.
As it happened, Antares would fly another 12 times before having to stand down again to be redesigned, but that is for a different This Day in Space entry.

New drug reverses severe fatty liver disease by repairing the gut
A promising new drug reversed severe fatty liver disease in animals by healing the gut, revealing a surprising new path toward treating liver damage.
- Michigan Medicine - University of Michigan

- Scientists have discovered that a potential new drug can reverse severe fatty liver disease in animal models by restoring gut health and blocking harmful substances from reaching the liver. The breakthrough could pave the way for new treatments for liver disease and potentially other serious conditions, including cardiovascular disease.
An experimental drug developed at Michigan Medicine has reversed a serious form of fatty liver disease in animal studies by targeting an unexpected source of liver damage: the gut.

The compound, known as DT-109, works by reducing harmful gut bacteria, protecting the intestinal lining, and preventing inflammatory substances from reaching the liver. According to findings published in The Journal of Clinical Investigation, this approach successfully reversed metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) in animal models, offering a promising new strategy for treating a disease that remains difficult to manage.

MASH affects approximately 7% of the world's population. It is a severe form of fatty liver disease in which excess fat accumulates in the liver, causing inflammation and cellular damage. Over time, the condition can progress to cirrhosis, which involves extensive liver scarring, as well as liver cancer and liver failure. Although treatment options have improved in recent years, effective therapies remain limited.

"We see clear evidence that DT-109 protects the gut epithelial barrier, reducing the systemic influx of harmful microbial products that are thought to contribute to MASH development and progression," said Eugene Chen, M.D., Ph.D., senior author of the study and Frederick G. L. Huetwell Professor of Cardiovascular Medicine at the University of Michigan Medical School.
"This compound shows benefits to the gastrointestinal system and has great potential as a treatment for MASH."
How Harmful Gut Bacteria Can Trigger Liver Damage

Chen's research team had previously demonstrated that DT-109, a glycine-based tripeptide, could improve MASH in animal studies. A tripeptide is a small molecule made from three amino acids, which are the building blocks of proteins. What remained unclear was exactly how the compound produced its protective effects.
The latest research provides an explanation, revealing how changes in gut bacteria can set off a chain reaction that damages the liver and how DT-109 can interrupt that process.
Before examining the drug's effects, the scientists confirmed an important contributor to MASH: excessive growth of Clostridium perfringens, a bacterium that produces ammonia inside the intestines.

When ammonia levels rise, they can damage the gut's protective inner lining. Normally, this intestinal barrier helps prevent potentially harmful substances from escaping the digestive tract and entering the bloodstream.

As the barrier weakens, however, toxins and other products generated by gut microbes can travel to the liver. Once there, they can provoke inflammation and activate immune defenses in ways that worsen liver damage.

One response involves the excessive activation of CD8+ T cells, immune cells that normally help the body destroy infected or abnormal cells. When these cells become overactive, they can contribute to the inflammatory processes associated with MASH.
The findings help explain why a disease centered in the liver can be strongly influenced by events occurring elsewhere in the digestive system.
Experimental Drug Repairs the Gut and Protects the Liver
Through a series of experiments, researchers discovered that DT-109 disrupts this damaging cycle by improving the intestinal environment and reinforcing the gut's protective barrier.

In both mice and nonhuman primates, the compound reduced levels of Clostridium perfringens and lowered ammonia production in the intestines. These changes helped strengthen the intestinal lining, limiting the movement of harmful microbial substances into the body and reducing their potential to damage the liver.

The results were particularly encouraging in nonhuman primates, whose liver biology and gut microbial communities more closely resemble those of humans than those of mice. In these animals, DT-109 reduced liver inflammation and lessened the severity of MASH.
Together, the findings show how targeting harmful processes in the gut can produce beneficial effects in the liver, even though the drug acts primarily within the gastrointestinal system.

"DT-109 connects microbiota modulation with liver protection by restoring gut barrier integrity and limiting the systemic translocation of ammonia and other pro-inflammatory microbial products within the gut-liver axis," said Jifeng Zhang, Ph.D., co-author and research professor of cardiovascular medicine at U-M Medical School.
"We also found that DT-109 primarily acts in the gastrointestinal tract, but its reach stretches much further."

The gut-liver axis refers to the close biological relationship between the digestive tract and the liver. Substances absorbed from the intestines travel to the liver through the bloodstream, making liver health particularly sensitive to changes in gut bacteria and intestinal barrier function.
By targeting this connection, DT-109 may offer a way to address some of the processes driving liver inflammation rather than focusing exclusively on damage that has already occurred.
Potential Benefits Beyond Fatty Liver Disease
Researchers believe the compound's ability to protect the intestinal barrier could make it useful against other conditions involving inflammation and metabolic dysfunction.
Previous research has shown that DT-109 can reduce the formation of atherosclerotic plaques and prevent vascular calcification in nonhuman primates.

Atherosclerotic plaques are deposits of fat and other substances that accumulate inside artery walls, potentially restricting blood flow and increasing the risk of cardiovascular problems. Vascular calcification occurs when calcium builds up in blood vessel walls, making them less flexible and contributing to cardiovascular disease.

These findings suggest that DT-109 could eventually have applications in treating both liver and cardiovascular conditions, an important possibility because metabolic disorders often affect multiple organs.

The researchers are also interested in whether the compound could help people with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), a group of chronic conditions that includes Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.

Because problems with the intestinal barrier are associated with several gastrointestinal disorders, a treatment that strengthens this barrier might have benefits beyond protecting the liver. However, additional research will be needed to determine whether DT-109 is effective against these conditions.
A Promising Treatment That Still Needs Human Trials

Despite the encouraging results, DT-109 remains an experimental treatment. Its ability to reverse MASH has been demonstrated in animal models, but researchers have not yet established whether it can safely and effectively produce similar benefits in humans.

The next phase of research will involve further evaluation of the compound, with the goal of advancing it toward clinical trials. Those studies will be essential for determining its safety, appropriate use, and potential effectiveness in patients.

"This study presents novel evidence about the pathogenesis of MASH and provides excitement about a therapeutic avenue to explore for a condition that remains difficult to treat," said Elliot Tapper, M.D., Academic Director of Hepatology at Michigan Medicine.
"What patients with MASH need is a safe and effective therapy capable of improving their liver and heart health - of course we are excited about these developments."

The discovery highlights an important shift in how scientists are approaching fatty liver disease. By addressing harmful gut bacteria and restoring the intestinal barrier, researchers may be able to protect the liver through a treatment that acts primarily outside the organ itself.

If future human studies confirm the benefits seen in animals, DT-109 could offer a new therapeutic option for patients with severe fatty liver disease while potentially addressing cardiovascular complications as well.

Chen is also an inventor of DT-109. The University of Michigan holds the patent for the compound and has licensed it to Diapin Therapeutics. Both Chen and the university have an ownership interest in Diapin, which supplied DT-109 for the research and is continuing its development.
