NASAâs Roman Space Telescope exceeds expectations by nearly 30%

- NASAâs Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has exceeded expectations after engineers made incredibly tiny adjustments to sharpen its view of the universe. By moving a mirror just one-sixteenth the width of a human hair, the team helped bring its powerful instruments into near-perfect alignment. Romanâs Wide Field Instrument now produces image quality nearly 30% better than predicted, promising exceptionally sharp cosmic surveys.

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is performing even better than scientists anticipated after engineers completed an extensive series of tests and precision adjustments. The work has brought the observatory's powerful instruments into exceptionally sharp focus, with its main camera system now delivering image quality nearly 30% better than predicted.

The achievement marks an important step toward the telescope's ambitious mission to investigate dark matter, dark energy, and other mysteries of the universe. Even the smallest improvements in optical precision could help Roman capture clearer images during its sweeping surveys of the cosmos.

"All of Roman's sweeping surveys will rely on the Wide Field Instrument," said Dave Hickey, a Wide Field Instrument systems engineer at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. "Many of the mission's primary goals, like studying dark matter and dark energy, wouldn't be possible without it, so it's both exciting and a huge relief to see that it's working well!"
NASA Puts Roman's Powerful Camera System to the Test

Following the activation of the Wide Field Instrument in September, engineers began a comprehensive testing campaign to confirm that each component worked properly on its own and as part of the complete system.

Their first priority was examining the instrument's 18 detectors, each roughly the size of a sticky note, along with the electronics that operate them. The team then evaluated the element wheel, a rotating mechanism equipped with filters and other optical components. These allow selected wavelengths of light to reach the detectors and can separate incoming light into its individual colors.

Next came the instrument's internal calibration system. Engineers activated its light-emitting diodes, or LEDs, which function as adjustable light sources that can produce different colors and brightness levels under commands from Earth. By measuring how the detectors respond to these controlled signals, scientists can identify differences in sensitivity and make the corrections needed for accurate observations.

Engineers also tested the instrument's alignment mechanism and moved it from the deliberately unfocused position used during launch to the position expected to provide the sharpest images. They finished by checking the thermal control system, which maintains the temperatures required for the instrument's various components to function correctly.

"Calibrating an instrument is like tuning a piano or guitar before a concert," said Maxime Rizzo, a Wide Field Instrument systems engineer at NASA Goddard. "You adjust everything until it's just how you want it and then leave the settings alone so it performs consistently while you use it."
A Space Telescope Already Close to Perfect Alignment
While one group concentrated on preparing the Wide Field Instrument, another worked to refine the telescope's overall optical alignment.

The results were encouraging from the beginning. Roman's mirrors and other optical components were already positioned with remarkable accuracy, meaning engineers needed to make only minor corrections.

"The telescope's performance was excellent even before we began adjusting the alignment of all the mirrors and other optics, thanks to exceptional preparatory work done on the ground prior to launch," said Matthew Bolcar, Roman's optical systems lead at NASA Goddard. "All of the testing and modeling work done at Goddard and by contractors at L3Harris and BAE Space and Mission Systems left only small corrections for us to make to bring everything into near-perfect alignment."

Achieving that level of precision is especially challenging for a spacecraft. The forces experienced during launch can cause tiny shifts in sensitive equipment, and conditions in orbit differ significantly from those on Earth. Roman launched on August 30, carrying optical systems that had been meticulously tested before leaving the ground.

"Our ground testing couldn't exactly reproduce the environment Roman would experience in space, such as the absence of gravity," Bolcar said. "And there are also slight differences in temperature variations and moisture content. Despite those challenges, the recent assessments showed that our ground testing was excellent, with both instruments either matching or exceeding the performance we had predicted."
A Mirror Adjustment Smaller Than a Human Hair

Roman relies on an intricate arrangement of mirrors and optical components to collect light from distant cosmic objects and direct it toward its two scientific instruments. For the resulting images to remain sharp, the light must follow an extremely precise path.
Even a microscopic misalignment can affect how accurately the telescope brings light into focus.
Fortunately, Roman's optical system was already so well aligned that only incredibly small movements were necessary to improve its performance.

"We moved the secondary mirror by about one-sixteenth of the diameter of a human hair," said Alden Jurling, a senior optical engineer working on Roman at NASA Goddard. "This adjustment nudged the height of the secondary mirror above the primary. If we scale that height up to the height of the Empire State Building, the change in height is a little bit less than you would get by stacking a single U.S. penny on top of the tip of the tower."
Although nearly impossible to appreciate at a human scale, such a small adjustment can make an important difference when a telescope is designed to study objects across vast cosmic distances.

The team initially concentrated on Roman's Coronagraph Instrument, which had been producing images that were slightly out of focus. The problem was less severe than engineers had anticipated, making it relatively straightforward to correct.

The coronagraph now meets the team's demanding performance expectations. Engineers will continue refining its camera settings and determining the optimal configurations for its deformable mirrors, which can change shape to make extremely precise corrections to incoming light.
In the coming weeks, the team plans to test the coronagraph's ability to block unwanted light, an essential capability for observing faint objects near much brighter ones.
Once the coronagraph's focus had been optimized, engineers returned to the Wide Field Instrument for another round of adjustments.
Roman's Image Quality Exceeds Expectations by Nearly 30%
The final measurements revealed an especially impressive result. Roman's Wide Field Instrument achieved optical performance nearly 30% better than the team had predicted.

Before launch, engineers established an image quality requirement of approximately 90 nanometers RMS (Root Mean Square). This measurement describes the amount of optical error in the system, or how far the incoming light deviates from an ideal, perfectly focused wavefront.

To put that scale into perspective, 90 nanometers is roughly 1,000 times thinner than a human hair. At these tiny dimensions, even seemingly insignificant imperfections can influence the sharpness of astronomical images.
After the latest corrections, however, engineers measured an optical error of just 63 nanometers RMS, substantially better than the original requirement.

That improvement means Roman should be capable of producing even sharper images than its designers initially expected, strengthening its ability to carry out detailed observations across enormous regions of the sky.
"All of the images from Roman's cosmic surveys will be even sharper than we expected," Jurling said. "It's a great outcome from years of careful modeling, precision metrology, and testing."

With both scientific instruments meeting or surpassing their expected performance, Roman has cleared another important milestone in its preparation for routine observations. The results highlight the extraordinary precision of the telescope's design and offer a promising outlook for its upcoming investigations into the hidden structure and evolution of the universe.
This bird flies thousands of miles, but its wings have a catch

- Scientists have uncovered an unexpected trade-off in the wings of the European nightjar, a bird that migrates thousands of kilometers but sacrifices high-speed flight efficiency to hunt insects with remarkable agility. Even more surprisingly, it generates thrust on the upward wingbeat, a technique that could inspire new flying technologies.

A bird that migrates thousands of miles has revealed a surprising secret about how wings work. Scientists have discovered that European nightjars sacrifice flight efficiency for agility and use an unexpected wingbeat technique previously associated mainly with bats and insects.

The European nightjar (Caprimulgus europaeus) is a nighttime hunter that makes an extraordinary annual migration between Europe and southern Africa. Yet the wings that carry it across vast distances must also perform a very different task: helping the bird catch insects while flying slowly and making sharp turns.

Scientists at Lund University have discovered that these competing demands come with a surprising trade-off. Although the nightjar is built to handle long migrations, its wings are not perfectly optimized for efficient flight at higher speeds.
Why Nightjar Wings Sacrifice Efficiency for Agility
To investigate how nightjars fly, researchers studied the birds in a wind tunnel, recording their movements at different speeds and measuring the patterns of airflow left behind their wings.

The experiments revealed that the nightjar's broad wing tips, which likely help it maneuver during slow flight, become a disadvantage as the bird flies faster. At higher speeds, its wings generate lift less efficiently. Lift is the aerodynamic force that helps keep a bird airborne.
The findings challenge the assumption that birds traveling enormous distances must have wings optimized primarily for efficient long-distance flight.

"This runs counter to the intuitive image of a long-distance migrant as a perfectly optimized flying machine. Instead, the nightjar's wings appear to be a compromise between several different demands. The bird can fly slowly and maneuver while hunting, but the trade-off is reduced efficiency in lift generation at higher speeds," says Christoffer Johansson, associate professor at Lund University.
Scientists Discover an Unexpected Wingbeat Trick

The researchers also uncovered another surprising feature of the nightjar's flight. Even as the bird raises its wings during the upward portion of each wingbeat, it continues to generate thrust, the force that helps propel it forward.
This is unusual because such an active upward wing movement, known as an upstroke, has previously been linked mainly to the flight mechanics of bats and insects rather than birds.
The discovery suggests that animals with very different evolutionary histories may have developed similar aerodynamic solutions to the challenges of flying.

"What's interesting is that the same type of aerodynamic solution seems to appear in quite different animals. This suggests that the upstroke does not have to be merely a passive or lift generating part of the wingbeat. It can be actively used to generate thrust when the wings cannot be folded very much," says Christoffer Johansson.
What Bird Flight Reveals About Evolution and Flying Robots
The results offer a broader lesson about how evolution shapes animals that depend on the same body structures for different activities.

Rather than producing wings perfectly suited to one purpose, evolution can favor designs that balance several competing needs. For the nightjar, that means combining the ability to migrate across continents with the agility required to hunt insects at low speeds.
Understanding these compromises could also lead to improvements in aviation technology, particularly drones and other robotic aircraft that use flapping wings.

Like birds, these machines may face mechanical restrictions on how much their wings can fold during each wingbeat. Learning how nightjars generate thrust during the upstroke could help engineers develop more effective ways to move through the air.
Researchers now hope to determine whether this unusual flight mechanism is widespread among other birds and flying animals or whether it represents a more specialized adaptation.

"We now want to investigate how common this way of generating force is among other birds and flying animals. It could help us understand which aerodynamic principles are specific to the nightjar and which are more general. This knowledge may also inspire the development of new types of flapping aircraft," Christoffer Johansson concludes.

It's well known that alcohol has profound consequences on the way the brain works, and research shows that even low levels of the drug can damage your brain.
But how does alcohol actually cause brain damage at the cellular level?
In a surprising discovery reported in Immunity, scientists found that alcohol doesn't just interact with neurons.
New findings show the drug also affects immune cells in the brain called microglia, triggering them to dismantle the extracellular matrix that structurally supports brain cells.

"For years, alcohol's effects on the brain were largely viewed through the lens of neurons, and for good reason: alcohol acts directly on neuronal receptors," says neuroscientist and senior author of the study Dimitrios Davalos from the Cleveland Clinic.
"By following microglia in real time, we were able to see that they aren't simply responding to damage. They drive the detrimental changes alcohol causes in the brain."
Microglia are specialized immune cells that continually monitor and maintain the brain by detecting threats, clearing out dead cells and damaged tissue, and pruning neuronal connections.

To explore how microglial activity is affected by alcohol, researchers investigated a mouse model of heavy alcohol consumption, designed to mimic the effects of binge drinking and high-intensity drinking.

In experiments, mice were given an oral dose of ethanol, or repeated doses over consecutive days, and the researchers monitored the drug's effects on microglia and neurons in living animals using two-photon microscopy and other imaging techniques.
The researchers found microglia underwent significant changes in shape and activity within approximately one hour of alcohol being administered, prior to peak sedation from the drug.
The branches that extend from their bodies reduced in number and length, and their surveillance territory shrank, with the effects becoming more pronounced after repeated exposures to alcohol.
The researchers also observed microglia damaging the extracellular matrix, a network of structural molecules that supports brain cells and helps to enable stable communication between neurons.
In mice given alcohol, microglia began to engulf and digest components of the matrix, breaking it down and weakening the structure.
This, the researchers suggest, results in a loss of synaptic connections, contributing to neuronal dysfunction, and possibly some of the sedative effects of alcohol.
However, in a separate experiment using genetically engineered mice, the researchers disabled a protein in microglia called MyD88, which plays an important role in activating immune responses.
In animals that had their MyD88 gene silenced, alcohol exposure resulted in significantly less neuronal damage, reduced changes in microglial shape and activity, and less pronounced sedation.

In separate tests with these protected, genetically engineered mice, the researchers degraded the animals' extracellular matrix using an enzyme, and doing so brought back synapse loss, motor impairment, and sedation when the animals were given alcohol.
According to the researchers, this shows that the disruption of the extracellular matrix is a key, causal process that directly produces some of alcohol's damaging effects on the brain.

While the primary findings were shown only in experiments on mice, a separate analysis of human brain tissue sourced from six deceased people with alcohol use disorder showed signs of extracellular matrix disruption compared to controls, which suggests a similar kind of microglial-driven brain damage may happen in people who abuse alcohol.
That could make MyD88 a strong therapeutic target for future research, and possibly beyond the effects of alcohol too.
"We discovered a specific neuroimmune route that alcohol activates, but it's possible that other drugs can turn that pathway on as well," Davalos says.
"My lab is looking into how we can target microglia or protect the brain's ECM to prevent or limit brain damage, from substance use and possibly even other neurological diseases."
For thousands of years, a mysterious army has stood vigil – silent and impassive in the dark, never wavering from their solemn duty.
They are the warriors of the Terracotta Army, carefully crafted 2,200 years ago in China to guard the tomb of Emperor Qin Shihuang.

The work is exquisite – at first glance, the thousands of warriors look identical, but look closer, and you'll find an astonishing variety of faces, hairstyles, and armor, a breathtaking display of craftsmanship.
Traditionally, archaeologists have assumed that the entire army was built by adult men.
New research reveals that this assumption may be wrong.

The sculptors – whose work endures long after the emperor they served – left their fingerprints in the still-wet clay, and it's those fingerprints that suggest men, women, and children likely all collaborated in the epic undertaking of the Terracotta Army.

"These findings challenge the long-held assumption that Terracotta Army production relied exclusively on adult male labor," write researchers led by archaeologist Xiaoxi Li of Emperor Qinshihuang's Mausoleum Site Museum, "providing the first quantitative biological evidence for a diverse workforce including women and children."
The Terracotta Army first came to light in 1974, after more than 2,000 years in darkness.
Farmers digging a well about 1.5 kilometers from the emperor's tomb site unearthed mysterious fragments of life-sized clay warriors.
What they had stumbled upon was an enormous underground army, whose full scale would take years to uncover.

The known extent of the Terracotta Army consists of thousands of life-sized statues – around 8,000 warriors, 130 chariots with 520 horses, and another 150 cavalry horses – but much of the emperor's vast necropolis remains unexcavated, and its full contents are still unknown.
Also largely unknown are the identities of the artisans who undertook this monumental work.
Relatively little research has addressed this question. Prior studies about the Terracotta Army have largely focused on how it was made, not who did the making.

So the theoretical assumption that it was men – the origin of which is unclear – was left more or less unchallenged, even though historical records show that women and children also worked in state-supervised workshops during the Qin dynasty.
A more diverse workforce was specifically documented in lacquerware production, Li and her colleagues note – but the composition of the workforce on the Terracotta Army remained an open question.
But traces of that workforce remained pressed into the clay.
Just as handprint analysis has revealed information about the artists of prehistoric times, fingerprints can shed light on who built the Terracotta Army.

The study is based on 36 of the warriors from a single excavation pit. An initial survey documented 91 fingerprints – 12 of which were later excluded because they seemed to be from individuals who left multiple prints.
That left 79 fingerprints for the full analysis.
These prints were left all over the warriors – heads, arms, armor, hands, collars, and even a foot – and they seem to have just been a byproduct of the making process.

"Surface impressions, accounting for 73 prints, were left during molding, shaping, and assembly processes when artisans pressed their fingers directly onto wet clay surfaces; these were most commonly found on figurine heads and arms, where artisans would grip components during attachment and smoothing operations," the researchers write.

"Relief impressions, comprising the remaining 6 prints, were formed when pre-formed clay decorations – primarily armor nails and waistbands – were pressed onto the figurine surface, and these were exclusively located on armor components."
You might think a single fingerprint can't tell much about an individual, other than that they were human (or three koalas in a trench coat).
You would, however, be mistaken, and the secret lies not in fingerprint size, but in the tiny distances between the lines on the print.
As the researchers explain, as a human grows, their fingerprint ridges become more widely spaced – but there's very little difference between boys and girls.
However, once people reach skeletal maturity, their growth levels off – and men tend to have slightly wider ridge spacing than women.
That means the average distance between the ridges – a measurement called mean ridge breadth – can offer clues about a person's age and sex.
But there's a catch: the measurements overlap considerably between different groups. For example, an adolescent boy might have fingerprints almost indistinguishable from those of an adult woman.

Rather than attempting to analyze each individual fingerprint and assign it an age and a sex, the researchers used an algorithm to estimate the proportions of different demographic groups represented across all 79 prints.

The researchers also adjusted their measurements to account for differences in fingerprint size between populations and for clay shrinkage during drying and firing, although it's important to note that their reliance on modern European reference data introduces uncertainty.
Nevertheless, the demographic spread came back far more diverse than previous assumptions allowed for.

Only 45 percent of the fingerprints, according to the model, were likely made by adult men. Another 32.7 percent were attributed to adult women. And the remaining 22.3 percent were attributed to children under the age of 15.

The presence of children in the workforce may not have been unusual. Historical records from the Qin dynasty describe a formal system of apprenticeships, in which young people learned their crafts under the supervision of experienced artisans.

According to the Yuelu Academy Qin slips – ancient legal manuscripts inscribed on bamboo – "The master artisan teaches well; thus an apprentice completes training in one year, a new artisan in two years."

It's possible, the researchers suggest, that younger apprentices were assigned relatively simple tasks, such as attaching decorative details to the warriors' armor, while more experienced artisans undertook the more technically demanding work.

There are, however, some important limitations to the findings. The 79 fingerprints came from just 36 warriors in one section of the vast archaeological site, and the proportions of fingerprints don't necessarily reflect the proportions of people who made them.
Inexperienced workers, for example, may have left more fingerprints than skilled artisans, whose handling of the clay was more practiced.
Still, the findings suggest that the Terracotta Army may have been the work of a far more varied group of people than previously imagined.
Future work could focus on expanding the fingerprint database to create a larger sample set that should tell us much more about who built the enigmatic Terracotta Army of Emperor Qin Shihuang.

"This biological evidence highly corroborates numerous historical records, vividly reconstructing the production scene in the Qin Dynasty's state-run workshops where men and women served together, and adult artisans worked alongside juveniles, who may have been helpers or beginners," the researchers write.
The research was published in the Journal of Cultural Heritage.
Like the surface of an ocean, the fabric of the Universe is constantly rippling with an infinitude of gravitational waves, propagating outward across the cosmos.
We can count, in triple digits, the number of these ripples we've detected to date – and most of them have been linked to collisions between black holes, the densest objects in the Universe.
But how do we know that every collision attributed to black holes is what it looks like? And what of the gravitational wave signatures we are yet to detect?
What if there's something else out there that can make the Universe sing? What if colliding wormholes can make a similar splash – and how would we recognize it when we find it?
For one particular kind of wormhole, at least, new simulations suggest collisions would be profoundly strange – and could leave distinctive signatures in the fabric of spacetime.

According to a preprint authored by physicist Nikita M. Shirokov of Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology and machine learning engineer Ilya Nachevsky of the Higher School of Economics in Russia, several things can happen when binary Ellis-Bronnikov wormholes interact – and most of them are extremely weird.
When you think of wormholes, you probably think first of science fiction – jump gates, hyperspace, tunnels through the cosmic backrooms that provide a shortcut from one region to another.

But, like many of the ideas presented in Star Trek and The Expanse, wormholes are firmly rooted in real scientific theory – a mathematical possibility emerging from Einstein's theory of general relativity, which describes gravity as the curvature of spacetime.
In theory, spacetime could be curved in such a way that two otherwise distant regions are connected by a tunnel, or throat – that's a wormhole.
Whether such a structure could actually exist in the Universe remains an open question.

You've probably heard the term Einstein-Rosen bridge. That's a type of wormhole that is non-traversable. A different model is the Ellis-Bronnikov wormhole – a traversable passage held open by something called a phantom scalar field.
This hypothetical field has unusual negative-energy properties that prevent the throat from pinching shut.
Traversable means something could go through it, but it does not mean stable, so whether a human should go through it is another matter.
This is particularly true for Ellis-Bronnikov wormholes.

Although the phantom scalar field can hold a wormhole's throat open, even a small disturbance can upset the delicate balance. The throat may collapse, forming a black hole, or begin expanding in a runaway process called inflation.
So you'd expect that if two of these volatile structures somehow cross paths, something pretty spectacularly destructive might happen.

To find out what those fireworks might look like, Shirokov and Nachevsky ran three-dimensional simulations of pairs of Ellis-Bronnikov wormholes, varying their initial separation, trajectories, and the properties of the phantom scalar fields that hold them open.
Depending on the configuration, the wormholes could attract or repel one another. Some passed close enough to interact before flying apart, their throats expanding dramatically in the process.
Others plunged towards each other – but instead of merging into one larger wormhole, something far stranger happened.
A common apparent horizon – similar to a black hole's event horizon – formed around both throats, enclosing them together inside a developing black hole.
This is where things got even weirder – because that apparent horizon then did something that black hole horizons aren't supposed to do.
As the phantom scalar field fell into the collapsing region of space, the horizon lost about 28 percent of its area.
Under ordinary circumstances, the surface area of a black hole's event horizon can only increase or stay the same, according to the black hole area theorem proposed by Stephen Hawking in 1971.

But that theorem relies on assumptions about the behavior of energy that the phantom scalar field violates. Its exotic negative-energy properties allow the simulated horizon to shrink rather than grow.

This doesn't contradict the area theorem, since the simulation involves an apparent horizon rather than an event horizon, and a field that violates the theorem's assumptions. But it's still a striking result.
Now, at this point, you're probably wondering what all this has to do with gravitational waves.
When massive objects such as black holes spiral inward toward a collision, their changing motion sends ripples through spacetime, like a boat's wake on the ocean. That's what gravitational waves are.
Wormholes, at least the massive Ellis-Bronnikov wormholes modeled in this study, should also generate gravitational waves as they move and interact.
But the researchers found that the resulting signals would be quite different from those produced by a pair of black holes spiraling toward each other.
The spiraling black hole pair has a distinctive signal called a chirp that grows stronger and higher in frequency as the two objects draw closer together.
By contrast, the researchers' simulations of wormhole encounters produced short, sharp bursts of gravitational waves.
The signal's precise shape and strength depended on whether the wormholes plunged toward each other or merely grazed each other in passing.
Interestingly, some of the closest flybys produced particularly strong gravitational-wave bursts, even without the formation of a common apparent horizon.
This doesn't mean that a gravitational-wave burst without a chirp is evidence of wormholes. Black holes can also produce such signals under certain circumstances.
One particularly unusual signal, GW190521, was detected in 2019 and has since been investigated as a possible signature of exotic spacetime physics.

That doesn't mean it was produced by a wormhole, and the new simulations don't establish a connection to that event. But it illustrates why understanding the possible signatures of hypothetical objects is worthwhile.

There's another catch, though. The researchers note that wormholes formed in the early Universe would produce signals stretched by cosmic expansion to frequencies far below those detectable by gravitational-wave observatories such as LIGO and the planned LISA mission.
For these particular signals to be detectable, the wormholes would need to form much later in cosmic history – and scientists don't currently know how that could happen.
Still, the Universe has surprised us before. And now, if we somehow do manage to record the signal of an Ellis-Bronnikov wormhole collision, we'll have a better idea of what we might be looking at.

Plants seem stationary: they don’t skip, fly or walk around. But that doesn’t mean they don’t move. The organisms bend their roots and shoots in response to stimuli such as water, light, salt and gravity. These responsive movements, called tropisms, are crucial for plants’ survival.
Now researchers have discovered a new way plants move, which they call “saprotropism”: the bending of roots to avoid dead or rotting plant tissue. The results were published in Science.

The discovery began with a failed experiment and an unexpected observation. Yuzhou Zhang, a biologist at Northwest A&F University in China, was studying how plants move in response to gravity in a laboratory in Austria when one of his agar plates became contaminated with airborne microbes. Just before he threw it away, he noticed something striking: almost every single one of the plants’ roots in the plate was bent away from the spoilage. The consistency “immediately made me wonder whether this was more than a random response,” Zhang says.

His team decided to investigate further. The researchers grew the common research plant Arabidopsis thaliana in containers, some of which were dotted with patches of rotting apple. The plants that encountered “decay zones” bent their roots to avoid the bad apple, whereas the ones in containers lacking decay grew straight through. Repeating the experiment with other plants, including tomatoes and wheat, yielded similar results—but an encounter with putrefying animal tissues had no effect. Zhang and his colleagues theorize that this reaction might help plants avoid pathogens, similar to the way unpleasant smells help animals steer clear of rotten food.

Saprotropism seems to operate differently than most other plant tropisms. “It does not follow the classical mechanism,” Zhang says. For example, gravitropism, or movement in response to gravity, and phototropism—in response to light—occur when plants redistribute the hormone auxin in their stems or roots, causing them to change their growth direction.

In contrast, saprotropism relies on a hormone called abscisic acid (ABA). When the plant roots encounter an area acidified by decaying plant matter—a chemical gradient distinct from that of animal matter—ABA builds up on the side facing the rot, encouraging growth in the other direction.

The work’s scope is impressive, says Chris Wolverton, a plant biologist at Ohio Wesleyan University, who was not involved in the study. He adds, however, that “there’s still a lot of open space in the signaling mechanism for more detail to get fleshed out.” At what point, for instance, does decaying plant tissue break down enough to become nutritious compost?
Zhang’s team hopes to fill those gaps in future studies. Ultimately the research could help illuminate how plants sense and interact with the world around them.
At the time of its Nasdaq debut in July, Bending Spoons was a little-known holding company out of Italy that owned older internet names like AOL, Vimeo, Eventbrite and Evernote.

Less than four months later, the Milan-based firm has emerged as a surprising home for former high-flying software startups that have been thrust aside by the artificial intelligence boom. Its M&A plan got a major boost this week from the most famous holding company on the planet: Berkshire Hathaway.

Berkshire, which Bending Spoons describes as a "longstanding inspiration" for its strategy, has now invested over $900 million in the company, including a $330 million stake disclosed on Wednesday. Wall Street loved the deal, sending Bending Spoons' stock up 41%, though some of those gains were lost later in the week, leaving the company with a market cap of about $30 billion.

"Berkshire's decision to add to its position just a few months after the IPO and at these levels provides another vote of confidence in the Bending Spoons model from one of the world's most respected long-term investors," wrote analysts at Mizuho, in a report after the announcement.

The other big news out of Bending Spoons this week underscores the flipside of the business: job cuts. In August, Bending Spoons announced it was buying workflow software provider Airtable for about $1.3 billion, or almost 90% below the company's peak valuation from late 2021. Bending Spoons said Monday that a "large portion of the pre-acquisition team" from Airtable would be leaving with "substantial separation packages." Layoffs were previously implemented at Evernote, Vimeo, WeTransfer and others in the portfolio.

For the technology industry, Bending Spoons' moves represent the latest example of how quickly fortunes are turning in the AI era, as new agents powered by large language models displace software developers and the products they built. With Anthropic and OpenAI marching toward trillion-dollar valuations, businesses are putting more valuable work in their hands at the expense of a host of software-as-a-service names, creating a phenomenon that's become known as the "SaaSpocalypse."

Shares of Intuit, HubSpot and Adobe are all down at least 30% this year, and a long list of private SaaS companies that were once venture darlings are now struggling to find capital, with the public market showing no appetite for IPOs. Last month, Bending Spoons agreed to buy collaboration software vendor Miro, once valued at $17.5 billion, for $1.36 billion.

"You're either like a hot thing or you're nothing," said Ethan Kurzweil, founder and managing partner at Chemistry VC and a veteran software investor. Kurzweil said he uses Airtable, and said there are plenty of good SaaS products on the market led by solid teams, "but they're not on the frontier anymore."

Bending Spoons was launched in 2013 by friends Luca Ferrari, the CEO, Matteo Danieli and Francesco Patarnello. A mobile app they'd created called Evertale failed to take off, and they used the $40,000 they had left to build an operating company instead of "products nobody wanted," according to the IPO prospectus.
Bending Spoons has announced all of its biggest deals in the last few years, beginning with Evernote in 2022, followed by Brightcove in 2024, and Vimeo, AOL and Eventbrite in 2025.
The company held its IPO on June 30, raising about $1.7 billion at $29 a share, and hit the Nasdaq the next day. The stock closed Friday at $47.07.

Prior to Bending Spoons' recent jump into enterprise software, some of the leading acquirers in the space over the past decade were private equity behemoths Thoma Bravo and Vista Equity Partners. Those firms were aiming to buy what they viewed as undervalued SaaS companies and, through a combination of cost cuts, efficiency improvements and rollups, turn them into assets that could be sold or taken public at a higher price.

Bending Spoons is using a different playbook. The company isn't looking for eventual exits but rather wants to generate profits from the businesses it buys, similar to the Warren Buffett model. But unlike Berkshire, Bending Spoons' focus is technology, and it's taking a hands-on approach with its own software, operations and personnel decisions.
Nick Mehta, former CEO of cloud software vendor Gainsight, said private equity firms are limited now because "they got their nose bloodied."
"They paid much higher prices and have so many troubled companies that it's difficult for them to take swings now," said Mehta, who sold Gainsight to Vista in 2020.
Thoma Bravo and Vista didn't respond to requests for interviews. Bending Spoons told CNBC in a statement that it hadn't been outbid for a target in "several years."
As the company started jumping into SaaS, Mehta said "Bending Spooned" became a verb in Silicon Valley, referring to companies getting scooped up for pennies on the dollar.
"Unfortunately, a lot of my friends in that game are stuck," Mehta said. "Investors want out but there are no buyers. Anything pre-ChatGPT is legacy now."
Lloyd Walmsley, an analyst at Mizuho, said Bending Spoons' model is distinct from the older buyout approach.

"I think there aren't a lot of people that do what these guys do in terms of the depth of operations and the willingness to make substantial product changes," Walmsley said in an interview. "It's not typical of traditional private equity firms to make anywhere near this level of change."
For customers of the companies that Bending Spoons buys, sudden price hikes can follow.

In April 2023, months after the Evernote acquisition, Bending Spoons lifted the annual personal subscription price to $130 from $70. Later, the company changed its offerings, charging $100 for its so-called starter plan and $250 for "Evernote Advanced," compared to the $170 it had been charging for the pro plan.
"My first reaction was like, Oh man, I guess I have to switch to OneNote," said Walmsley, referring to Microsoft's notetaking app. But he said he stuck with Evernote.
"They're really savvy at finding these things that they provide a lot of value, and the switching costs are really high," Walmsley said. "The price isn't that high relative to the switching cost."
Bending Spoons uses the profits from its portfolio companies for future growth, the "overwhelming majority" of which comes from doing more deals, Ferrari told CNBC in an interview on Thursday.
"There are certain opportunities for improvement we can unlock over the first few years, and then the business will have whatever organic growth is intrinsic in that market," Ferrari said.
For Berkshire and its fellow Bending Spoons investors, the bet is still unproven.

The products have to remain desirable enough that customers are willing to pay up at a time when AI is squeezing margins across much of the software sector. In its first earnings report as a public company in August, Bending Spoons said revenue more than doubled from a year earlier to over $700 million, with growth almost entirely driven by acquisitions, while net income climbed 171% to $177 million.

That was before the Airtable deal had closed and Miro had yet to be announced. In the coming quarters and years, Wall Street will get a clear picture of whether the firm's structure can revive software.
On the earnings call in August, an analyst asked whether Airtable represents a long-term shift in the M&A strategy towards enterprise.

Ferrari said that about half of Bending Spoons' revenue already comes from professional businesses, largely through Brightcove and Vimeo, which has an enterprise component. The focus on software of late, he said, has more to do with where he's finding value after a hefty selloff.
"Most enterprise SaaS businesses were valued at irrationally high levels until somewhat recently," Ferrari said. "We never saw those prices making any sense."
— CNBC's Ari Levy contributed to this report.
Investors may want to rethink their bond allocation and opt for managed futures exposure.
DBi's Andrew Beer suggests the popular hedge fund strategy could deliver a modern twist to traditional 60/40 portfolios.

"[Bonds have] been dead money for the entire decade," the firm's co-founder and managing member told CNBC's "ETF Edge" this week. "I fell in love with a strategy called managed futures because tactical is really good. Be nimble when other people's [portfolios] aren't."

Beer contends the managed futures strategy, historically only available to hedge funds, could counterbalance stocks better than bonds during periods of volatility, which has been moving higher due to recent worries surrounding debt and the artificial intelligence trade.
His reason: Managed futures exchange-traded funds can go long and short across global markets to position early against turbulent market events.

"You want something that has low correlation to both stocks and bonds, and something that will do well in crises," Beer said. "It's very, very hard to find a better hedge fund strategy than managed futures to accomplish that."

He helps manage the iMGP DBi Managed Futures Strategy ETF (DBMF). The fund replicates the performance of leading managed futures hedge funds inside a low-cost, liquid ETF, according to the firm's website.

"There's an existential crisis right now in strategic asset allocation and the model portfolio world," Beer said about the 60/40 approach. "I love my bonds … [but] I'm not making it a 40% allocation for something that is not adding to the rest of my portfolio."
As of Thursday's close, Beer's ETF is up almost 19% so far this year, according to FactSet data.
However, managed futures may not be a replacement for bonds.
According to NovaDius Wealth Management's Nate Geraci, bonds still have a place for diversifying a portfolio.

"I call fixed income the most challenging area in investing right now," the firm's president said in the same interview. "[Alternatives] fit in the sleeve of a well-diversified portfolio that includes stocks and bonds. But I don't think you just give up on the bond side of the equation."
Geraci added that investors should understand how alternative investment strategies like managed futures ETFs could interact with the rest of a portfolio.
These funds can outperform during volatile markets, but they may also have periods of underperformance.
"You have to let that work out over the long-term," said Geraci, who is also an ETF Institute co-founder. "To me it's just a balance. It's all about diversification."
When the economy and the market look shaky, gold and government bonds are the traditional places to park money. Lately, some investors have also been looking at something more rooted: timber.
The pitch is easy to like: a back-to-basics, natural asset that grows on its own, matures into a harvest and can be cashed in all while you use it to hunt, pitch a tent, or forage.

Institutions have been buying timberland at a rate of one million acres per year, according to Bank of America, and some financial advisors say individual investors, including younger Americans priced out of the housing market, are also taking a look at the asset class. But it is far from a rush, and investors who already own timberland caution that it may not be very profitable in the short term.

"Timber is a very low return investment. I have curtailed my investments," said Pat Dorn, founder of Anchor Investment Management, a fee-only advisory firm in Columbia, South Carolina, and a former chairman of the South Carolina Forestry Association. Dorn owns 2,500 acres of timberland in South Carolina's booming upstate region. Dorn said the problem is that right now more timber is being grown than is needed in a sluggish housing economy.
"Supply beats demand, and that causes flat prices. Timber is not an investment I would make currently," Dorn said.

Nationally, the Bureau of Labor Statistics' producer price index for logs, bolts, timber, pulpwood and wood chips ticked up in September, but prices have been mostly on the decline since summer 2022. This measures prices received by producers for those products, rather than timberland values or investment returns. Over the very long-term, prices have climbed substantially.
Financial institutions point to the asset class as one of interest specifically for the long-term investor.

Ken Shepard, head of specialty asset management at Bank of America Private Bank said that timberland is not a tactical asset class that can be easily entered or exited in response to short-term market conditions. "We view it as a strategic, long-term investment supported by several favorable secular trends, including the continued expansion of the timber industry in the U.S. South and growing demand for wood products beyond traditional construction uses," Shepard said.

For example, he said, demand for wood pellets used in bioenergy, while controversial, has increased significantly. In addition, timberland values are benefiting from strong demand from recreational and lifestyle buyers, providing support for land prices beyond the income generated from timber harvesting.

The National Council of Real Estate Investment Fiduciaries' Timberland Property Index, which tracks privately held U.S. timber properties owned at least partly on behalf of institutional investors, posted a total return of 0.95% in the second quarter of 2026, comprising 0.34% income and 0.61% appreciation.
Timberland managers dominate acquisitions
Bank of America's 2026 outlook reported that the one-million-acre annual pace of buying is a three-year streak of dealmaking it expects to continue.

According to Bank of America, timber managers acquired 55% of all acres that changed hands in 2025 against just 15% sold. Institutions are playing the long game. Large timberland managers buy for pension funds and endowments that can wait decades, and that can make bets on a longer-term recovery in a currently slumping U.S. housing market that will be good for lumber pricing. But a private owner living through today's market sees things differently.

Dorn pointed out that timber companies buy less mature trees for pulpwood, which goes into paper towels or notebook paper, and those trees can take 12-14 years to mature. The chip-and-saw variety of trees take a little bit longer, while the big prize, timber cut for houses, can take 25 years. "That is where the top value is," he said.

According to Dorn, what landowners are paid for standing timber varies depending on what the trees are used for. Pine pulpwood consists of trees ground into paper and packaging, while pine sawtimber is made up of larger trees cut into lumber for homebuilding. Meanwhile, hardwood sawtimber, consists of oak and other big trees used in flooring, furniture and pallets. Each product feeds a different set of buyers, so one can climb while others fall.

South Carolina Forestry Commission data show statewide average pine pulpwood stumpage prices, what buyers pay landowners for standing timber, fell from $5.67 a ton in the third quarter of 2025 to $3.79 in the third quarter of 2026, a decline of about 33%. Pine sawtimber prices fell about 6% over the same period, from $22.78 to $21.47 a ton, while hardwood sawtimber prices rose about 40%, from $16.04 to $22.52.

Historically, pulpwood has been as high as $12 to $18 a ton, according to Dorn, and twenty years ago, soft timber was in the $35-$40 range. He said those prices could make a comeback if the housing market ever recovers, because pine sawtimber is cut into lumber for new homes, so its price tends to follow home building.

Strategically placed, timber may not be a bad investment, according to Dorn, though that would be because of the land itself more than the timber. "The return is in the land, not the timber," Dorn said.

He advises anyone thinking of investing in timberland to scout for prime parcels of land located outside growing metro areas that may be poised to pop as the local population keeps spreading. "If one hopes to buy land near growing metro areas and holds on to it, timber is a reasonable way to keep it earning something — a very low return — while you hold that land," he said.

Michael Martin, a timber owner in western New York and vice president of market strategy at brokerage firm TradingBlock, says timberland can be a good long-term investment but the reality of being an owner belies the romantic image of acres of untouched timberland. It is not as passive an investment class as it may seem to be.

Direct ownership is highly illiquid and comes with management costs, property taxes, harvesting expenses, exposure to local timber markets, and risks including wildfire, pests, disease and trespassers hunting or cutting trees.

And when it is time to harvest timber, you need to make sure you are getting the best deal. "If you simply go with a small local outfit without getting competing bids, you don't always know if you're getting the best price," Martin said.
He also said timber prices are very local and can impact whether it's a solid investment.
"I am constantly checking stumpage reports because timber prices are extremely local. An oak tree in western New York may have a completely different value from one in the Adirondacks," Martin said.
In addition, partial timbering every ten years or so has barely covered the property taxes. "At the end of the day, I barely break even," he added.
Some in local real estate and investing markets say younger buyers are curious, though firsthand evidence is hard to find.

"As a millennial and a realtor, I understand the appeal. I've thought about buying timberland myself," said Jake Kennedy, a Nashville-based realtor, noting that his generation has lived through the dot-com crash, the Great Recession, a pandemic, huge swings in housing and now inflation. "One lesson from all of that we have learned is that scarcity matters when it comes to places to park your money," Kennedy said, adding as examples that more IPOs can be announced or new crypto created.

"But you can't manufacture another 500 acres of land," Kennedy said. "Timber itself is a resource that takes decades to grow. And there is something reassuring about owning an asset that is tangible," he added. But he also cautioned that timber's durability doesn't mean profitability. Trees can be temperamental and subject to many variables.

The people Kennedy has spoken with see timberland as a relatively safe place to park money, he said, because demand for timber products isn't going away. "In the meantime, yes, hunting is a common activity while owners are waiting for the investment to grow and mature, literally," he said.

"I don't think my generation is suddenly giving up on houses and becoming timber barons. However, I do think we are a lot more interested in alternative places to store wealth than previous generations might have been," he added.
Timber ETFs offer access to the asset class

For many millennials, homeownership has become increasingly difficult due to elevated home prices, higher mortgage rates, and limited inventory in many markets. "As a result, some investors are looking for alternative ways to participate in real assets and potentially build equity without purchasing a home directly," said Nadeem Kassam, chief investment strategist at Marnoa Private Wealth Counsel.

Outside direct or institutional fund ownership, there are timber ETFs and timber-focused funds that provide exposure to a theme that is closely tied to long-term housing demand and construction activity, though they remain highly niche investments in an ETF market now valued in the trillions of dollars.
Kassam pointed to the iShares Global Timber & Forestry ETF (WOOD), with roughly $260 million in assets, and the Invesco MSCI Global Timber ETF (CUT), which has roughly $30 million in assets.

"The investment case is supported by persistent housing shortages across many parts of the U.S. and growing bipartisan support for policies aimed at increasing housing supply and improving affordability. If these efforts lead to increased homebuilding over time, demand for lumber and wood products could benefit," Kassam said.
But he noted that investors should understand that timber ETFs are not a direct investment in timberland. Neither ETF owns trees.

"Most own publicly traded companies involved in timber, forest products, wood manufacturing, and other parts of the housing value chain," Kassam said, explaining the advantage is liquidity and accessibility, but returns will be driven by more than just timber prices.

WOOD's largest holdings include Weyerhaeuser, a major timberland owner, alongside Brazilian pulp maker Suzano, Nine Dragons Paper and West Fraser Timber. CUT is weighted toward paper, packaging and materials makers such as Svenska Cellulosa, UPM, Stora Enso and Avery Dennison. WOOD has drawn about $73 million in net inflows over the past year, according to ETF Database.

"For investors who are priced out of the housing market, timber ETFs may offer a way to participate in the long-term housing and construction story through a diversified, liquid investment vehicle. The key is recognizing that you're buying exposure to businesses that benefit from housing-related demand, not a direct ownership stake in land or residential real estate," Kassam said.

Junyi Liu, professor of economics at Soka University of America, who studies international and development economics, said he is not seeing evidence of a boom, but that timberland does have some unusual characteristics as an alternative asset.

"Returns can come from biological growth, timber prices, and land appreciation, and owners sometimes have the option to delay harvesting when timber prices are unfavorable," Liu said. But for retail investors, Liu added, it is quite different from "the simple 'trees grow while you wait' investment story."
Street Fighter is leading the box office battle in its opening weekend as Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything draws big crowds, while Whalefall has trouble making a splash.

Coming in on the lighter side of Paramount Pictures’ projected sum, Street Fighter grossed $13 million on Friday, including Thursday previews, and will open with around $31 million domestically for the weekend from 3,575 North American theaters. Marking the first release in Paramount’s distribution deal with Legendary, the studio had been expecting a debut in the mid-$30 millions for director Kitao Sakurai’s feature adaptation of the Capcom video game. Noah Centineo, Andrew Koji and Callina Liang star in the $82 million-budgeted movie focusing on a combat tournament.

Street Fighter earned a B- CinemaScore from audiences and has struggled to win over critics, holding a 42 percent approval from Rotten Tomatoes reviewers, along with an audience score of 82. In his review for The Hollywood Reporter, critic Frank Scheck called the film a “jumbled tonal mess” and “only sporadically entertaining.”

Jumping out to an impressive start from 855 North American locations is A24’s You Can See Everything, as the documentary about Theranos founder Holmes’ life leading up to her prison sentence collected $5.5 million Friday, including Thursday previews, as it opens with around $12 million. The studio reports roughly 750 sellout screenings for the weekend and plenty of lines in cinemas as the movie heads to one of the best-ever starts for a non-music doc, besting the $7 million opening earlier this year that gave Melania the biggest launch for a film in the category in over a decade.

Directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim‘s You Can See Everything is a strong draw for younger audiences, with the turnout showing 75 percent of ticket buyers in New York and Los Angeles as under age 35. Critics and general attendees alike have marveled at You Can See Everything, and it boasts a 99 percent approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes from both reviewers and audiences. It stands as the highest-rated Letterboxd title ever with a 4.8 score.

Universal Pictures’ Other Mommy could be heading for third place with around $7.8 million, marking a sharp decline of about 72 percent after earning a D+ CinemaScore in last weekend’s debut. Jessica Chastain stars as a sinister spirit appearing in a girl’s closet in Rob Savage’s horror offering that heads to an estimated domestic sum of $43.3 million after opening at No. 1 a week ago.

Getting a quiet start is 20th Century Studios’ Whalefall, which is expected to reel in around $7 million from 3,065 North American theaters. This is below the $11 million that the studio was projecting for director Brian Duffield’s survival thriller starring Austin Abrams as a scuba diver swallowed by a sperm whale. Earning a B CinemaScore from audiences, Whalefall carries a $60 million budget for the feature adaptation of Daniel Kraus’ 2023 novel.

Whalefall holds a 71 percent critics approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, with an 82 score from audiences. THR chief film critic David Rooney wrote in his review that the movie is “just not batshit crazy enough to be much fun.”

Coming in just below that on the chart is Focus Features’ Sense and Sensibility, which took in $3.2 million on Friday, including Thursday previews, for an estimated opening of $6.7 million from 2,545 North American theaters. Earning an A- CinemaScore, director Georgia Oakley’s adaptation of Jane Austen‘s esteemed novel stars Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles in the story of the Dashwood sisters navigating life after their father’s death.

Carrying a budget in the mid-$20 millions, Sense and Sensibility holds a 75 percent approval from Rotten Tomatoes critics and an 89 score from audiences. Rooney noted that the film “seldom steps out from the long shadow of Ang Lee’s enchanting 1995 retelling.”
Additionally, Netflix releases buzzy Oscar contender La Bola Negra in four theaters, with this title marking the first time ever that the streamer will publicly release box office returns.
The options heading to theaters next weekend include Clayface, Wildwood, Klara and the Sun, Ali G: Who Iz I? and Wicker.

TikTok has banned the entire Musk film account, citing political content that violates its policies. The move, which comes just as the Alex Gibney’s investigation into Elon Musk expands to more than 470 screens across North America, raises concerns about Big Tech suppression that the very film seeks to expose.

Distributor Bleecker Street was informed Friday afternoon a “permanent suspension” was coming. The entire page disappeared from TikTok’s platform shortly after. The film company had been planning to spend ad money to boost certain posts; that will no longer happen.

A spokesperson for the distributor confirmed that TikTok reps had informed them of the suspension and noted “disappointment” in the timing. After grossing $70,000 in four theaters in New York and Los Angeles in its first weekend of release, Musk is now playing in dozens of cities this weekend. The spokesperson said the company is in the process of appealing the move; even a reversal, however, could still prove costly if it doesn’t come during a weekend window when many people are likely to see the film.
A TikTok representative did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Musk goes deep on a number of its subject’s actions and companies, which Gibney spent more than three years investigating. The film devotes a large portion of its second half focusing on Musk’s political activities with DOGE and beyond. It also centers on his acquisition of Twitter, which Gibney suggests was done to control the digital public square, adding an element of potency and irony to the TikTok move.
An official message from the company to Bleecker Street noted a “level of severity with political-policy violations” and said that “some violations trigger immediate suspension.”

It was unclear, however, what those violations were. Bleecker Street had just posted two new pieces of content before the suspension came. In one, a cheeky ad about what to do during intermission of the nearly four-hour doc, on-screen text suggested deleting your X account, “chat about a fascist hellscape” and “”switch your seats if they are too far to the right.”
A second post suggested seeing the movie “before it gets shut down,” adding a further element of irony to the social ban.
The Musk TikTok account account has garnered more than 10,000 followers since going live, an uncommonly high number for an individual documentary.

TikTok has no official affiliation with Elon Musk, though it is partly owned by Larry Ellison, who gets a rough moment in the doc when a text from him offering to pay billions to the mogul to help finance his Twitter acquisition is shown. TikTok has been more resistant to Musk content than some of its competitors, refusing to reverse its position again accepting an ad for the trailer even after Meta and Google/YouTube did just that. X, of course, been unwilling to accept any advertising for the film.
Larry’s son David is set to release Gibney’s doc when his newly acquired HBO, which financed the film, puts in on the platform in 2027.
The year arguably belongs to Anne Hathaway. But it’s been a pretty banner 10 months for a particular co-star from one of the actress’ five theatrical releases.

Patrick Brammall leveled up in 2026. After opening himself to his widest audience ever by playing the love interest to Hathaway’s Andy Sachs in the nearly $700-million grossing Devil sequel, he made a rare turn as a dramatic leading man in Apple TV+ thriller Last Seen. And, in September, he released the third and final season of Colin From Accounts — the romantic comedy he created with and starred alongside his wife, Harriet Dyer.

Colin From Accounts follows strangers Ashley (Dyer) and Gordon (Brammall) as they fall in love after share responsibility for a dog (the titular Colin) Gordon runs over with his car and leaves permanently handicapped. In a funny way. The Australian series was a success in the duo’s home country, a juggernaut in the U.K. and a sleeper hit in the United States. And the fact that its end coincides with an onslaught of other work is not lost on Brammall, whose career, with a few exceptions, has been largely defined by his work in the Southern Hemisphere. “I think we’ve all had a year, the same year, 2026,” he says, when I tally his credits, before surrendering and turning it into a bit. “Yeah, it was mine. You’ve all been having my year. It’s pretty mental, isn’t it?”

Brammall breaks into a few bits over our early October conversation, one where he covers the significance of Colin From Accounts, his daughter’s disinterest in the fact that he voices a character on Bluey and how he still has no idea what was really going on with his character on the bonkers Paramount+ supernatural drama Evil.

You’ve worked a lot in Australia and now a lot in the U.S. as well. I suspect that there are many aspects of television that are done differently. How, in you speaking to like studios and platforms, can you compare the response to pitching a show that starts with a dog getting hit by a car?

Australia and the U.K. didn’t have a problem with it. That’s funny. These two strangers meet at an intersection, she flashes her nipple, he gets distracted, he hits a dog. It’s hilarious. In America… not so hilarious. There’s even a website, doesthedogdie.com. So in when we were pitching it over here, we had to start with, “The dog’s fine and he’s very well cared for.” And you do meet his previous owner at the end of the first season. That guy was an asshole. Colin’s got a much happier life.
The show title obviously worked in the end, but it’s not the easiest sell. Many people assumed it was a workplace comedy. Was there ever any pushback on the name?

There was a bit of pushback. Because Colin from Accounts does not sound like what the show is. Our only alt title was Dog with Wheels, which wasn’t very good either. We liked the name because these two people, in that first episode of season one, what they connect about is naming the dog Colin from Accounts. They have a shared sense of humor. They’re plugged into the same frequency. That serves as their foundation. I think lot of people who found the show either were always going to watch it or just stumbled on it. They watch that first episode and they feel like they’re in on the joke. It does set the tone in many ways. On the other hand, terrible title.
You and Harriet wrote every episode. Have you ever worked in a traditional writer’s room?

Only once — and even then it wasn’t that traditional. I did a show called No Activity for CBS All Access. We did the show in Australia first, and it was just Trent O’Donnell and myself. We created it, and it was largely improvised. We just had outlines. But for the U.S. version, the studio was like, “Hey, we love it! Write full scripts, please.” That’s not really the show, but they’re paying, so we did it. Trent and I ran a writer’s roombut were not very good at it. (Laughs.) People came in and I found it really inefficient. It was a fun time and you’d order lunch and you’d have your Le Croix, but I found it a very inefficient way to write something. Having said that, there were a lot of great ideas that came out of it. It was just so lumbering.

So Colin From Accounts wraps up. You have this well-received dramatic turn in Last Seen. And you were in The Devil Wears Prada 2. It’s a real strong year for you. Have you noticed any previously closed doors opening up?

A couple of doors have opened, and it’s probably a result of the combination of the lot. I know Colin opened doors, because I wouldn’t have the offer for Prada because the writer (Aline Brosh McKenna) and director (David Frankel) were huge Colin fans. I don’t have people smashing the door down, but also that’s a little bit intentional. The last eighteen months have been so crazy. Our youngest is 20 months old. We’re just back in L.A., steadying the ship and just being a family for a minute.
I mean, you’re working in all of these different countries with children who are not at, shall we say, a fun age to travel with.

Dude, tell me about it. Just going back for Christmas to Australia is a siege. Recently, our eldest did something like six schools in eighteen months. She didn’t know where the fuck she was. So when we got back to L.A., it was like, let’s just stop for a minute.
Is is it easier for her to transition into a new school with the clout that her father voices a character on Bluey?

It would be if she accepted that I voiced a character on Bluey. She will not. I tried to tell her once, because I’m a sad man. I’m like, “Hey, do you recognize that voice? Is that dad?” And she just looked at me like, “Don’t ruin this for me.” Like, fuck off, mate. (Laughs.) She has a point. What am I doing trying to ruin Bluey for her? I’ll leave her to love Bluey for as long as she can before I ruin it for her.
I heard that when you sent in your audition tape for Last Seen, you had to have your hands tied to your to your body to keep you from gesticulating. Please explain.

My dear friend Kirsty McGregor, who cast last scene and was the casting director on Colin from Accounts, said “Hey, I’m working on this. I’ve put your name in the mix. They want to see a tape. This is the only tape that’s happening. So everyone’s gonna see it, so don’t fuck it up.” I put it down one morning, sent it off and, a couple of days later, she said, “Look, it’s great. I’ve got some notes. This isn’t Colin from Accounts. Stop gesticulating. Like, just be still. This needs to be a leading man. This is a thriller.” This is is some practical screen acting advice, which I haven’t had for 30 years. So, one Sunday morning, we’re out in the back office and Harriet filming. She’s wearing a dressing gown. I’m doing the thing and I’m trying to be good be still. She says, “Stop flapping your hands around!” Then she takes off the cord from her dressing gown and and ties my hands to my side. And that’s the tape that we sent. Everyone is like, “Fantastic! You’ve got the job.” And I thought, fuck, how can I do this job without a dressing gown cord?
Semi spoilers for anybody who didn’t watch you in Evil, Michelle and Robert King’s Paramount+ drama, but at a certain point… I had no idea what the hell they were doing with your character.

I love this show, but your character is this absentee husband who pops in and out after climbing expeditions. You were never a series regular. And at some point, you’re just locked in some attic getting a sludge transfusion from your apparently satanist mother in law? Did they explain this to you?

That show is so good. And those last couple of seasons, I would just show show up with the script and go, “Well, what the fuck’s happening to me now?” It was such a fun job, because I was recurring, this husband character who comes in and out. So, periodically I would fly to New York and do two, maybe three episodes a season. And I was the absent partner and father of these five three girls? Four girls? There were a lot of girls. Initially, I was very invested in the character. Like, “What am I doing? What does this mean?” Eventually, I was like, “This show is fucking crazy.” It goes mental. I was kidnapped by Michael Emerson’s character. He and and Christine Lahti, they were putting something into me or taking blood out. I can’t remember! And then in the final season, I’m in a mental institution having an affair with Anna Chlumsky.

I lost track. I had this final scene with with Katja Herbers. She was smashing stuff and telling me what’s what, and I looked out the window like, “I guess that’s the end of Andy’s story.” (Laughs) It was crazy and and the most fun set and story. I really loved it. That show was underrated.

Just curious, now that Colin from Accounts is over, you employed your canine co-star, Zak, for years. Dogs can be a lot like child actors. Are you going to stay part of his life and make sure he doesn’t spiral?

I’ve done everything I can for that dog. Now I just have to let it go. You can only keep a dog out of rehab so many times before you say, “Go with God. It’s up to you now.” He’s off the rails, and he knows it. He’s on a collision course with something and it’s not good. No, Zak is one of the best boys. He was more professional than many of the humans there — so much so that Harriet sometimes we’d have to get like a bit of turkey on us so that looked like he was doing something. He was very comfortable in the wheelchair, but he’d just sit there.
So calm. I did always clock it when he wagged his tail.
Was he on beta blockers? I don’t know. But good for us.

From career milestones to new music releases to major announcements and those little important moments, Billboard editors highlight uplifting moments in Latin music. Here’s what happened in the Latin music world this week.
