“It’s always been a dream of mine to play such an iconic venue,” Miley wrote on social media just hours ahead of her Hollywood Bowl performance on Friday night (Oct. 16).

It was a funny reminder for longtime fans who have seen the child actor ascend to pop star heights; while Miley has been around and iconic for so many years, it’s really been the last few in which her career has been celebrated more widely.

At the 2024 Grammys, she won her first award (actually, two) for her Billboard Hot 100 No. 1 smash “Flowers,” taking home record of the year and best pop solo performance. In 2025, she joined Spotify’s exclusive Billions Club, delivering a hits-filled set in Paris to perform her biggest songs including “Wrecking Ball” and “The Climb.” And earlier this year, she celebrated the 20th anniversary of Hannah Montana with a Disney+ special and rare media blitz.

Already this year, she dropped Cyrus from her stage name — joining mononymous legends like Madonna, Cher and Beyoncé. And now, in her own words, she is living out a longtime dream of playing Los Angeles’ famed venue the Bowl.

Miley last performed a full set four years ago, in Mexico for over 150,000 fans (the Bowl’s capacity is 17,500). Since, she became a frequent guest at Chateau Marmont for intimate, invite-only sets but has otherwise remained absent from the stage. Needless to say, anticipation and fervor was at an all-time high for her first of two sold-out Bowl shows (the second is Sunday, Oct. 18).

From the live debut of Bass Persuades standouts to the sing-alongs for generational hits like “We Can’t Stop,” “Party in the U.S.A” and “The Climb,” here are the seven most notable moments from Miley’s major live return.

- The Bass Persuades Opening Hat Trick Given that Miley has released three albums since her last full performance, there was a lot of catching up to do. But, given that these two Bowl shows were branded and marketed in promotion of Bass Persuades – her latest album that topped the Billboard 200 for one week — it was only natural to start there. Following a black and white spoken-word video interlude of Miley — the first of a few that were sprinkled throughout the show — she opts to open with Bass standouts “Orbit,” “Different Religion” (for which she plays electric guitar and welcomes collaborator and opener Model/Actriz back on stage) and “Bass Persuades” into its remix. Hearing the new material live helps it snap into place within her catalog, cementing the album overall as a grungier, bassier big sister of Plastic Hearts. Miley followed the trio of Bass selects with “Handstand” off Endless Summer Vacation, saying: “You didn’t expect this one, did you?” But we should have — as the song, which she shares was the very first she ever wrote with her partner Maxx Morando, was basically breadcrumbing the more experimental sound she’s continued to explore.

- Honoring Her Aunt Dolly: “Me and Dolly Are Eternal” As a photo of a young Dolly Parton fills the venues’ screens, the crowd softly chants “Miley, Miley” while her back remains to the crowd. Once she finally turns around, compact mirror in hand, she says, “She told me to check my make up,” before sitting on the edge of the stage. “So many reasons that I wanted to perform at the Hollywood Bowl,” she says with a shaky voice and her head down. “Above every single one of them is that I only got to see Dolly Parton live in concert one time in my entire life — and it was here.” Miley continues to share a story of how she wanted to go and enjoy, only to have the experience ruined by Dolly informing the crowd that she was seated among them (Dolly also insisted on entering her own show to the Hannah Montana hit “Best Of Both Worlds”). Despite the funny memory, Miley can’t help but tear up again as she says, “Me and Dolly are eternal,” adding that she feels her presence now more than ever. “I’m going to see her again and I can’t wait,” she continues, “because I fucking miss her.” Miley then performs “Jolene” as she has before. And to begin her next song ,“Walk Of Fame,” she fittingly flashes an image of Dolly’s Hollywood star. The song’s outro says it best: “You’ll live forever.” Just another thing Miley and her Aunt Dolly have in common.

- Wayne Coyne’s Surprise Appearance Following another video interlude in which Miley talks about Woodstock as a reminder that “you can be lost and exactly where you need to be,” heads quickly turn toward a B-Stage in the center of the crowd where the one and only Wayne Coyne (of The Flaming Lips) is standing. He begins to sing the band’s hit “Do You Realize??” before being joined by Miley, who welcomes him with a big, long hug and then joins in on the final chorus. After it wraps, she says Coyne is “family” and shouts out Miley Cyrus & Her Dead Petz, which she calls “my favorite album that I’ve ever made.” Coyne sticks around for one more song, as the two dive into “Karen Don’t Be Sad” off that project. “I’m having so much fun,” says Miley as Coyne exits. “I didn’t know if I was gonna… you never know.”

- Her Sentimental Moments (And Brief Reunion With Twerking) Dipping into her catalog got Miley feeling reflective again — she had already acknowledged early on how grateful she was to her fans for understanding her need for a balanced life that doesn’t include endless touring. Still speaking from the B-Stage, she shares that she has a new fish that Maxx named: “I have to have those things that give myself balance, she says. “Yeah, I was really excited to perform for you all at the Hollywood Bowl, but to be honest, I’m equally as excited about the new fish. And that’s what I love about my life, is I get both…I’m experiencing everything I’ve ever wanted.” She then says that “it’s been a long ride,” noting her near-20-years-long career “of this metamorphosis – and you have not skipped a beat. It’s been steadfast and deeply felt.” Then, surely and only as a gift to fans, Miley sang the first verse of “We Can’t Stop” before letting it play out — and even attempts to twerk along, saying “let’s see if I can still do it.” She still can, even in pants and blazer.

- Her Emotional Walk Through the Crowd: “I Don’t Want My Mom to Worry” Instead of stealthily returning to the main stage, Miley instead takes an emotional walk through the crowd to get back. Once she does, she dives right into her emotional banger “Wrecking Ball,” which she sings while clutching a heart-shaped frame of Dolly. “That was Dolly’s favorite song of mine, so I had to bring her with me,” Miley says. Then, clearly still reeling from the up-close experience she just had with the crowd while walking through it, she offers insight into the emotional toll of such a seemingly simple act. “I’m ok, I don’t want my mom to worry,” she says, glancing side stage. “I do want to say, it is a lot for me… feeling how much passion and love you radiate to me, and I appreciate you so much.”

- The Nostalgia-Fueled Backend: “Some Of My Old Ways” By this point, it’s clear we have reached the “Best Of” section of the set. Having heard “We Can’t Stop” and “Wrecking Ball,” Miley fittingly throws in the newer but heavily reflective “Used To Be Young” followed by “The Climb” and then “Party In the U.S.A.” During “Party,” the stage more or less becomes one with confetti and streamers and a final appearance from Coyne, who returns with a giant silver balloon sign that reads: “F–K YEAH HOLLYWOOD BOWL.” As Miley quips: “Some of my old ways.”

- Giving the Bowl Its “Flowers” Ad-Lib For her two-song encore, Miley leads with “Let’s Get Married,” walking onstage holding hands with Morando. A portable drum kit has been moved center stage, at which he sits and plays while Miley lovingly sings beside him. After the song, as he returns to his proper kit a bit behind him, Miley declares: “This song is one of my personal favorites,” and delivers her mega hit “Flowers.” (The juxtaposition of the two back-to-back is especially representative of how much of Miley’s life has and continues to play out in public, from a messy divorce to finding love again.) “Flowers” live ad-libs have become a playful and expected bit, with the best to date having been at the 2024 Grammys when she sang through a wide smile: “Started to cry but then remembered… I just won my first Grammy!” Tonight, she updates the lyric to her latest achievement, beaming as she sings: “Started to cry but then remembered… I sold out the Hollywood Bowl!” And not just once, but twice. And not just because she wanted to, but because she crafted a show and its parameters around her own comfort and happiness. Not only can Miley buy her own flowers, but she can make her own rules, too. Just as she always has. And sure enough, the people will come. Just as we always have. Oct. 17 (UPI) -- Pope Leo XIV has been discharged from the hospital Saturday after successful lung cancer surgery and plans to lead the noon prayers Sunday from the window of the Apostolic Palace.

Dr. Luigi Carbone and Prof. Stefano Margaritora said Leo had blood tests and a chest X-ray in the morning, which confirmed that he was healthy enough to leave Rome's Agostino Gemelli Hospital, Vatican News reported.
The pope, 71, was diagnosed with cancer Tuesday and had part of his right lung removed during surgery to remove a nodule, his doctors said.
Carbone and Margaritora said the pontiff had adenocarcinoma "as suspected by the pre-operative tests" he had before the surgery. It's the most common type of lung cancer.
Before leaving the hospital, he celebrated Mass in a room on the 10th floor of the hospital for staff.

As Leo left the hospital, he was greeted by 13-year-old Vavara, a Ukrainian girl who survived cancer. She had met him once before, while she was undergoing treatment for cancer, and he had hugged her.
This time, she wanted to return the well-wishes. Vavara and her family traveled from Castellamonte, in the province of Turin, where they now live.
Varvara told Leo that their hug had given her "the strength to overcome the illness that, fortunately, I have now beaten."
She said she "wanted to come to Rome to pray for him beneath his window and return that important embrace."
"You, too, will overcome this moment and continue your work of spreading the Gospel," she said.

The pope is planning to travel to Latin America Nov. 6-17. He is scheduled to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, where he lived and worked for years. But the Vatican said it's cautious about his travel plans, CNN reported.

"We need to see how the Pope feels once he is discharged -- what his state of health is -- and based on that, he will decide whether to keep or cancel his trips," Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Holy See Secretary of State, told reporters Friday.

Oh, Canada. The Great White North is the latest country to contemplate legislation that could essentially mandate backdoors and increase data retention in encrypted services. The proposed changes have prompted the Canadian anti-censorship company Psiphon VPN—which keeps millions of Iranians online during repressive internet shutdowns—to say it will leave the country if the bill passes. And Psiphon is not the only one.

Encrypted messaging app Signal has said it would exit the Canadian market because the legislation would require unacceptable changes to its open source projects. Apple and Meta have criticized the bill, and DuckDuckGo and NordVPN say they would consider pulling their services, too. But as countries around the world contemplate similar legislation, even larger questions begin to emerge about which states or regions could differentiate themselves as being safe havens for privacy services if global hostility to encryption continues to rise.

It’s been maddening and disturbing to see more and more democratic countries around the world propose changes to their surveillance and data collection laws, with the aim of giving cops and intelligence agencies greater powers to access people’s information. Governments already have broad digital surveillance powers and investigative tactics to solve crimes that involve encrypted data, but legislative proposals almost inevitably include provisions to expand this access even more—mandating additional logging and what amounts to backdoors or intentional flaws in encrypted products, which cryptographers and security engineers have consistently said cannot be built safely. Truly everyone who understands the issue has said it as much for decades. Yet policymakers return again and again to the idea, somehow expecting a different conclusion or a new breakthrough that will make it all possible.

“There have always been some officials within certain agencies that tend to view technology as a crime scene in and of itself, and it becomes a myopic point of fixation where access is desired,” says Kate Robertson, a senior research associate at the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab. “But that type of siloed thinking forgets that technology needs to be the secure operating platform for hospitals, for banks, for national security agencies, for police services themselves to protect victims who report private information to them.”

In recent years, the UK and Australia have introduced sweeping surveillance reforms that can compel companies to break their encryption. Other encryption-threatening proposals have also emerged in the EU, France, India, Ireland, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, and others. While not all measures have passed into law or been enacted, the hostility is clear.

First proposed in 2025, and partially revised due to blistering criticism from tech companies and civil society, Canada’s C-22 bill can broadly place requirements on tech companies, including those outside of Canada, to introduce “technical capabilities” that allow data to be accessed for law enforcement purposes. Like many such bills, C-22 says that companies will not have to introduce a “systemic vulnerability” into their systems. But opponents have pointed out that any capability to access end-to-end encrypted data amounts to a backdoor that could be discovered and abused by anyone. And this risk is only heightened even more by the ease with which anyone can now use AI tools for reverse engineering and system mapping.

“Companies could be asked to introduce vulnerabilities, build backdoors, bypass, weaken or otherwise defeat encryption,” members of the US House Judiciary and Foreign Affairs committee said in a May letter to Canadian officials.

In addition to potential impacts on encryption, C-22 also includes provisions that could require companies to retain metadata about user activity, something that many privacy focused services (including VPN services from Psiphon and DuckDuckGo) intentionally avoid. As a result, these companies say, they would be forced to change their business models to collect data they do not need or want to collect about their users. And researchers say that such product changes would diminish user trust while increasing the potential for widespread surveillance.

“If you are asking and requiring for this infrastructural change—that they retain metadata by default—it is creating a surveillance capability within a tool that didn’t have it,” says Afsaneh Rigot, the founder of the De|Center, a research organization that aims to reduce the risk of technological harms. “There are contexts like Iran and other contexts globally, who all of this has a trickle effect on. It's not going to stay in Canada because these types of laws always get copy pasted around the world.”

As more countries contemplate such laws, developers focused on privacy and anti-censorship tools are increasingly casting around for safe jurisdictions to operate in. But this still doesn’t solve the problem of reaching users in all countries around the world and for now, there are no sure bets.

“Changing your headquarters isn’t much of a plan B when the law follows your users, as C-22 would,” says Joseph Lorenzo-Hall, security portfolio lead at the Internet Society. “The strongest protection is holding as little user data as possible, but ‘we don’t have it’ is no defense if governments can force you to start collecting it. A safe haven needs more than favorable winds in strong encryption. It needs laws that let companies keep their privacy promises and defend them against foreign threats to confidentiality and integrity.”

Summer is officially over, along with its allotment of free sunlight. You might be sad about this, but your indoor plants might be even sadder. A good LED grow light can replicate sunlight with full-spectrum light and day/night cycles, keeping plants lush and thriving even in a dark, windowless corner or basement.

I have no fewer than 40 houseplants in my home at any given time, as well as a fair number of grow lights, and what I've found to be important for a general consumer (i.e., someone not doing that kind of indoor grow) isn't necessarily certain colored light wavelengths but whether a grow light is easy to live with in your house.

Many grow lights are more or less going to serve the same purpose, so what you really need to know is this: Is the light so bright that it's disruptive? Does it require complicated installation? Is it easy for kids or pets to knock over? The grow lights recommended below are ones that WIRED staffers have lived with for months, if not years, and have found them both effective and easy to integrate into our lives.
Also be sure to check out our guides to the Best Indoor Gardening Systems, Best Gifts for Plant Lovers, and Best Kitchen Composters.

Photosynthetic photon flux Ddensity, or PPFD, expressed in micromoles per square meter per second (μmol/m²/s), is a measurement of how much light reaches your plant that's usable for photosynthesis. In general, the higher the plant's energy needs, such as producing a flower or a fruit, the higher the PPFD number you want. Though different lights have different height requirements given the plants they're made for, for standardization purposes, I measured the PPFD of each grow light at 18 inches with the Photone app and a light diffuser. Keep in mind these measurements are general and approximate.

Some of these grow lights I bought myself, with my own money, before I even began working at WIRED. Others were owned by staffers and recommended to me. I also have press samples from other guides I worked on, which I liked so much I ended up keeping around.

For the traditional grow lights, I tested them at home under normal-life conditions. I put them where they'd fit, tested their timers, and noted whether or not they were dimmable. I also measured each light's PPFD (see above) and noted whether certain lights could be daisy-chained for more extensive coverage.

Up to four Vego lights can be daisy-chained together, and the five preprogrammed modes (Seeds, Leafy, Fruits, Herbs, Microgreens) have varying intensities and automatic built-in off periods to simulate nighttime. I have not found this light especially disruptive, especially since it's easy to turn on and off with the button on the back.

WIRED commerce SEO director Stewart Savin used these lights to start her garden earlier this year and had 138 successful germinations across 144 seedling cells. An automatic cat feeder may just change your life. No more begging at 4 am. Plus, it can give you peace of mind while you're away from your fur baby. As seen with the rise of automatic litter boxes and pet tracking, technology has made it so we can closely monitor our pets without doing a lot of the manual labor normally involved.

Gravity-fed automatic dry-food dispensers were invented nearly a century ago, but today most automatic cat feeders use Wi-Fi and connect to a phone app that lets you set a schedule or feed on demand from afar, all while monitoring your pet’s eating habits. Newer models have taken this tech further, like the Petkit YumShare Dual-Hopper 2 Automatic Feeder With Camera ($170), which has a built-in, AI-enabled camera that analyzes the remaining food in the bowl and stops dispensing to prevent overfeeding. Automatic wet-food dispensers—our top pick in this category is the Petlibro Polar Smart Wet Feeder ($170)—are relatively new, often using ice packs or mini-refrigeration cooling systems to keep the food as fresh as possible.

Automatic feeders are also helpful for pet parents who want to monitor their pets’ health, maintain specialized schedules, or foster healthier eating habits. (A customizable automatic cat feeder can help with the endless gorging-vomiting cycle many cats struggle with.) Nearly all of the automatic cat feeders on this list are marketed toward cats, but some can be used with smaller dogs, and I’ve noted these below.

I don't love having food and water so close, since cats prefer them separate to prevent cross-contamination in the wild. I'd recommend this basic option if you're on a budget and need a temporary solution for when you're out of the house (and don't mind not having a connected app).

Closer Pets C200 2-Meal Automatic Pet Feeder for $50: This automatic feeder is super simple, which is both its weakness and its strength. It’s essentially two shallow plastic containers with stainless-steel inserts (both dishwasher-safe) and tamper-resistant lids that lock and automatically open using an old-school egg-style timer that runs on an AA battery rather than electricity. Although the container has an ice pack to keep the wet food cool, after one night it lost virtually all of its coolness. There’s a lid-link clip attachment, a small piece of plastic that links the lids to ensure they open at the same time, which is super helpful for owners of two cats like me. I wish the timer were electric so I could program it to the exact time I want it to open, rather than guesstimating the timing on the little marks. However, this is a simple solution to help make sure both my cats are given wet food without me having to wake up at the crack of dawn.

Oneisall Cordless WiFi Automatic Cat Feeder for $53: I had high hopes for this cordless feeder, which boasts a rechargeable battery with a 100-day life and an integrated app, but it's just too unreliable. Through the app, you can program up to 10 daily meals (in 1-12 portions each), monitor pets' eating habits, and customize meal calls. Unlike other apps, you can't choose portion size; instead, you have to multiply the number of servings. The app gave me constant problems and would often disconnect from the feeder and be unable to reconnect to WiFi. Luckily, I was able to program meals via the screen and buttons, but it would've been much nicer if the app had worked reliably.

Catit Pixi Smart 6-Meal Feeder for $86: Like others on this list, the Catit Pixi wet and dry feeder uses ice packs to keep wet food fresh and rotates meals among six compartments on a set schedule. The schedule can be programmed via the app or adjusted on the feeder itself. At this price point, the app shouldn’t be this limited and glitchy. The schedule is available in military time only, and the app is extremely limited—you can only set the meal schedule for the same day. When I wanted to do only two to three meals a day spread over two days, I had to reschedule the meals for every new day. The feeder didn't keep it cold enough to spread the meals out, and the wet food was not at a safe eating temperature. At this price point, just get the Petlibro Polar wet feeder.

Catit Pixi Smart Cat Feeder for $112: Kibble is stored in the feeder’s body, but it lacks a window to visually check food levels. The meal-planning calendar shows only a week at a time, and although it should repeat daily based on the schedule, I found that some days had no schedule despite setting one up. The Pixi also doesn’t tell you how much food was dispensed; it just refers to it as a “portion”—I manually measured and found the portion was less than a tablespoon of kibble. After using it continuously for more than a month, I found it was extremely glitchy and almost never reliably stuck to the programmed schedule, sometimes skipping meals altogether. This feeder is potentially dangerous, and I'd caution pet parents against relying on it.

Closer Pets C500 for $77: This automatic wet and dry feeder can schedule up to four pre-portioned meals (and one meal given manually) and opens them on a timer using three AA batteries (sold separately). The user sets the four times they want the bowls, which have ice packs underneath, to rotate. The bowls are quite deep and narrow, and they aren’t super easy for cats to reach, which could cause whisker fatigue. Although there are two relatively large ice packs, when I checked on the feeder after a night’s sleep, the packs weren’t very cold. This may be OK for kibble, but wet food was kept at unsafe temperatures, and my cats couldn't reach all of the food.

Automatic feeders are great for pet owners who want to help manage their pets’ weight and monitor eating patterns. Plus, they allow for a lot more control and precision, so owners can learn exactly how much their cat is eating and when. Because cats are naturally more nocturnal, many have the annoying habit of waking you up in the early hours, demanding food. These feeders allow you to set up a schedule that fits their schedule better without inconveniencing yours.

Of course, it’s never recommended to leave pets alone for long periods, but these automatic feeders give more peace of mind and are much healthier for your pet than leaving a huge amount of food out for free-feeding while you're away for the night. Simply put, it’s an easier way to feed and monitor your cat’s health with less work for you, the human.

I have two rescue cats, ages 4 and 5, and they eat two wet-food meals a day, along with small amounts of dry kibble throughout the day. Vets (and TikTokkers) have successfully persuaded me to move toward a primarily wet-food diet, which has a higher water content. This provides more moisture in their diet, which helps with potentially life-threatening problems like UTIs, which are especially prevalent in male cats. I still like to give smaller dry-food meals throughout the day to satisfy their need for crunch.
For dry food, I use Hill’s Science Diet, and for wet food, I use Friskies Shreds. (Yes, only Shreds. Fellow cat owners will understand.)

I set up the feeders, noting ease of setup, potential problems, and app navigation. I also tested various schedules and manual feedings in the app, documenting any issues. I used each feeder for at least a week, if not longer.

Although cats are generally considered less high-maintenance than dogs, it’s still not advisable to leave your cat alone for extended periods. In dire circumstances, you can leave a cat alone for 24 to 48 hours with scheduled feedings and a clean water source, but it’s not ideal—especially for cats with health issues, kittens younger than a year, or very elderly cats. Although these feeders are automatic and meals can be scheduled in advance for multiple days, our pets still need their human pals around for enrichment, care, and, well, love.
For the first time in two years, the works of one of Spain’s most celebrated painters, Joaquín Sorolla y Bastida, are back on public display at his namesake museum in Madrid.

The Sorolla Museum partially reopened this week, boasting a nearly 20,000-square-foot expansion. That includes new exhibition spaces, an auditorium and storage for the museum’s 1,394 paintings and roughly 5,000 drawings by Sorolla—the world’s largest collection of his works.

“After the remodeling, the Sorolla Museum will have a new, expansive personality,” Enrique Valera, the museum’s director, tells the Art Newspaper’s Alexandra F. Coego. “We didn’t have a space like this before, and it will allow us to expand our cultural programming for every type of visitor.”

The museum is centered around Sorolla’s home and studio, where the artist, who was born in Valencia in 1863, worked and lived with his family from 1911 until his death in 1923. The museum opened to the public in 1932, after his widow’s death.

The home makes for an enchanting space. “Stepping into the seductive confines of the compound, where Sorolla lived with his wife and three children, is like entering one of the artist’s luminous paintings,” Tony Perrottet wrote for Smithsonian magazine in 2008. “Sorolla’s easels stand ready, as if he had just left for a siesta; his palettes, brushes and half-used paint tubes are close by.”

But because the house was designed for a small family, it struggled to keep up with the demands of being a public museum that, in 2023, the centenary of the artist’s death, saw a record 345,000 visitors. Since the 1930s, the museum has undertaken partial measures to adapt to increased visitation, including redesigning exhibition halls and installing climate control to protect Sorolla’s works. “Nevertheless, all these interventions were only partial in scope,” per the museum’s website.

That changed four years ago, when the museum began an ambitious overhaul and expansion project costing some €13 million (roughly $14.5 million), according to Todo Alicante’s Rocío Mendoza. Work on adjacent properties bought by the Spanish Ministry of Culture began in 2022. The main museum shut its doors in 2024. The expanded galleries are now open, although the house and studio will remain closed for years to come.
“The restoration of the studio home is being carried out with surgical precision and will take years. But the goal is to recover its original essence,” Valera tells Todo Alicante.

The expansion was built with the same architectural spirit as Sorolla’s home studio—an ample use of wood and emphasis on natural light—giving it a cohesive feel with the larger museum. It also lives up to Sorolla’s nickname, “the master of light,” which he earned for his paintings of sparkling beaches and other outdoor scenes.

The expanded museum has an interior courtyard and garden roofs that designers hope will help the space blend in to its residential surroundings. A glass wall in the expanded building, which currently frames a view of the under-construction studio home, will later be converted into a connective threshold that physically and conceptually bridges the museum’s past and present.

The reopened museum’s first temporary exhibition, “Behind the Artist’s House: The Architecture of the Sorolla Museum, 1905–2026,” debuted this month and runs through early January. It tells the story of the house’s design, which Sorolla personally oversaw, and the subsequent evolution of the Sorolla Museum.
“Behind the Artist’s House: The Architecture of the Sorolla Museum, 1905–2026” is on view at the Sorolla Museum in Madrid until January 10, 2027.

Microplastics have been found throughout the human body, including the brain, lungs and blood. Past studies have identified associations between the tiny particles and various health issues, such as cardiovascular disease, dementia and reproductive problems. But the exact way they might contribute to these problems has been unclear.

Now, scientists say they’ve found an answer: Microplastics appear to generate highly reactive molecules when they interact with water. If the same effect were to happen in our bodies, microplastics could lead to oxidative stress, which damages cells, and inflammation. The findings, published in the journal Nature on October 14, challenge the idea that plastics don’t easily react with other substances and point to how they can cause harm to humans.

“We’ve long assumed that plastic itself is inert, and that any harm from microplastics comes from the chemicals added to plastics or the pollutants that stick to them,” Lisa Patel, a physician at Stanford Medicine Children’s Health who wasn’t involved in the study, tells Everyday Health’s Becky Upham. “This study suggests the surface of the plastic particle can be chemically active on its own.”

Bulk plastics are generally thought of as durable and chemically resistant, but that “needs to be reconciled with the toxicity of their fragmented microscale forms,” the authors write in the study. When plastics degrade into microplastics—pieces smaller than a pencil-tip eraser—their surface-to-volume ratio goes up. For example, if a credit card gets broken down into bits just ten microns in diameter, or around one-tenth the thickness of a sheet of paper, that increases its surface area more than 200 times, explains study co-author Wei Min, a chemist at Columbia University, to Payal Dhar at Scientific American. The more exposed area, the more chemical activity.

To better understand how these tiny fragments might generate chemical activity, Min and colleagues examined particles of widely used bulk plastics, including polyethylene, polypropylene, polystyrene, polyvinyl chloride and polyethylene terephthalate.

Analyses revealed that when microplastics interact with water, they spontaneously generate unstable molecules known as reactive oxygen species. Because plastic repels water, or is hydrophobic, the surrounding water can’t form its usual hydrogen bonds. So, contact between the two substances results in electric changes that can help create volatile molecules called hydroxyl radicals.

Microplastics are therefore “like a permanent little factory” that generates this reactive oxygen species, Min tells Evan Bush at NBC News. “Our cells are 60 to 70 percent water, and therefore this effect could be ubiquitous.”
Did you know? Contributions to climate change
Researchers reported in May that microplastics swirling in the atmosphere might be heating up the Earth by absorbing sunlight and warming the surrounding air.

These harmful hydroxyl radicals were even produced when the team mixed microplastics with mouse blood, although the effect was smaller than in water. In response, some red blood cells seemed to change shape, and their activity levels shifted. “We do show immediate biological consequences,” Min tells NBC News. “Proteins get damaged. Cells get damaged.”

However, the exact size and mechanism of this effect is still unclear, and it may depend on how our bodies get rid of microplastics, Min tells Jo Marchant at New Scientist. “How much plastic is in a regular human being? We have no idea right now.”

What’s more, adding a chemical called a surfactant that weakens the forces holding water molecules together reduces the generation of hydroxyl radicals, the team found. And some substances in the body, such as certain lipids, have this property.

“Microplastics hit your lung, and they are surrounded by surfactants immediately,” Matthew Campen, a biochemist at the University of New Mexico who wasn’t involved in the study, tells New Scientist. “In most situations that I can imagine in a biological system, they will be surrounded by those lipids. The big concern is [whether] this is getting worse over time, and we really need to get a handle on what the health effects are, or could be, so that we can avoid exposures.”

Still, the findings give scientists a new way to look at plastic pollution’s impacts, says Martin Wagner, a toxicologist and a biologist at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology who wasn’t involved in the work, to Scientific American. “It implies microplastics themselves are a source of oxidative species ... and oxidative stress is not a secondary effect of exposure.”

A previously unknown drawing by the 18th-century Venetian artist Canaletto is heading to auction in England. The pencil and brown ink sketch—only just authenticated—is one of Canaletto’s famous capricci, imaginative art works that blend detailed studies of real architecture into fantastical scenarios.

“His capriccio pictures form a small portion of Canaletto’s oeuvre, and this drawing includes many elements typical of this genre: monumental architectural structures, ruins, water and groups of figures, known as staffage,” art historian John Rolfe tells Artnet’s Richard Whiddington in an email. “They show brilliant observation, an eye for detail, but also imagination, fantasy and drama.”

Mallams, an auction house in Oxford, England, will sell the capriccio later this month. It was authenticated by Charles Beddington, an art dealer, historian and Canaletto expert. Canaletto likely composed this scene between 1746 and 1755, during his stint in England, as a sketch for a painting that was later auctioned by Christie’s in the 1990s.
Born in Venice in 1697, Giovanni Antonio Canal, more commonly known as Canaletto, was a vedutisto, or “view painter.” He became famous for highly detailed depictions of his hometown.

“Canaletto would often sketch out his scenes in a mathematical way, drawing the lines of the architecture in pencil with rulers before going over it in pen,” according to Katherine Gazzard, a curator at Royal Museums Greenwich. In fact, Canaletto’s cityscapes were so accurate that he was once accused by a biographer of tracing buildings with a camera obscura. (Researchers disproved this rumor with the help of infrared technology in 2017.)

The recently authenticated drawing depicts a ruined Renaissance-era arcade with two crumbling arches spanning a canal. Before them is a rickety wooden footbridge. Embedded in the riverbank silt is old debris, including a stray carriage wheel. Harsh light and shadow add depth to the scene, and everyday characters are scattered throughout.
“Silhouetted against the light sky, a mother and child step cautiously across the bridge,” Rolfe says in a video from Mallams. “Pose, character and costume, captured in a few quick strokes.”

From the Italian word for capricious or whimsical, a capriccio is an architectural fantasy of the landscape genre. These artworks depict fabricated scenes amid real structures, such as columns from the Roman Forum or Venetian archways. Capricci became popular among Italian artists during the Baroque period, with practitioners including Francesco Guardi and Giovanni Paolo Panini.

While Canaletto’s fame is today associated with his more straightforward cityscape views—one such painting of Venice sold for $30.5 million earlier this year—“the painter himself may well have been more proud of his capricci, works of the imagination being held in higher esteem, particularly by his Italian contemporaries,” per Mallams.

An inscription on the back of the capriccio drawing says it is “a Present from Sig Canal d Canaletti,” suggesting the artist gave it away as a gift. It is thought to have then belonged to Charles Burney, an 18th-century British composer, and passed down in his family for generations.

“Original paintings and drawings by Canaletto rarely come to auction,” Rupert Fogden, Mallams’ director of fine art and pictures, tells the BBC’s Ethan Gudge. “We are expecting a significant amount of interest from both private collectors and institutions worldwide when it goes under the hammer this autumn.”

When temperatures spike, California redwoods slow down photosynthesis, new research has found. This finding has serious implications for the long-term survival of the iconic trees in a warming world, and their role in storing carbon from the atmosphere.

California redwood (Sequoia sempervirens) forests are among the largest aboveground carbon stores on the planet. These towering trees are native to central and northern California, and evolved to take advantage of the region's historically mild weather. In recent decades, their range has contracted significantly. But climate change is threatening the health and function of these forests.

The region has seen significant warming in recent decades, and faces more frequent extreme heat days, with temperatures spiking above 100 degrees Fahrenheit (37 degrees Celsius). Now, in a new study, published Sept. 22 in the journal JGR Biogeosciences, a team of researchers has shown that California's renowned redwoods are struggling to photosynthesize in the heat.
Photosynthesis is the process used by plants, algae and some bacteria to turn sunlight into energy. It chemically converts carbon dioxide and water into sugars and oxygen.

"These trees adapted to grow in really temperate environments, so no one had really looked at the impact of heat on photosynthesis," study first author Lily Klinek, a doctoral candidate in the Plant Optics Lab at the University of California, Davis, told Live Science.

From 2022 to 2024, Klinek and colleagues measured how the leaves of redwoods in Garcia River Forest in Mendocino County responded to the heat. Once or twice a month, the researchers took three different California redwood leaf samples and measured their fluorescence and temperature.

A plant's molecules can use absorbed light in three ways: for photosynthesis, dissipated as heat, or reflected as light (florescence). Fluorescence is a proxy measurement to understand photosynthesis in the plant, Klinek said.

The researchers wrapped a fourth leaf in tinfoil for 20 minutes to put it in a state of "rest" before taking the same measurements. "When they're in a state of rest, we expose them to a pulse of light that’s in the wavelength they would use for photosynthesis to see what would be their maximum photosynthetic rate," Klinek said.

They found that on hot days, the leaves exposed to sunlight were up to 18 degrees Fahrenheit (10 degrees Celsius) hotter than the air temperature. "That's a huge difference and indicates that the leaves are stressed to the point where they can't thermoregulate effectively," Klinek said.

Many plants' leaves manage their temperature and photosynthesis by opening or closing their stomata, which are tiny pores on their surface. These stomata (from the Greek word for mouth) regulate the amount of carbon dioxide entering the plant, and how much oxygen and water vapor it releases. Lower carbon dioxide intake leads to reduced photosynthesis, meaning the plant has less energy.

The large differences between air and redwood leaf temperatures suggest that the leaves had closed their stomata to avoid losing water from evaporation during hot conditions and consequently overheated, Klinek said.

To further investigate the impact of heat on leaf physiology, the researchers took California redwood leaf samples back to the laboratory and exposed them to a range of temperatures while they were in water. Despite their access to water, the leaves still photosynthesized less as they got hotter, even though their stomata were open, Klinek said.

This shows that heat imposes direct limitations on redwood photosynthetical capacity, rather than indirectly decreasing that capacity by causing stomatal closure, the researchers wrote. The finding indicates that redwoods' ability to photosynthesise and store carbon will decrease as temperatures rise.

"It is not only stomatal closure that is causing reduced photosynthesis," Lucy Rowland, an ecologist at the University of Exeter in the U.K. who was not involved in the study, told Live Science in an email. "These trees are already suffering from the direct effects of heat on their photosynthetic systems."

The finding has serious implications for the future of redwoods and similar plants. "The points at which this damage becomes irreversible remains really poorly understood, but is something which is really essential to understand if we want to predict how our future climate is going to impact plants," she said.
The next step in Klinek's research is to move beyond leaf physiology to understand these thresholds on the trees and their ecosystems as a whole.

"We're not sure to what extent the effect that we saw is a reversible stress response and if they are sustaining damage from this constant stress," she said. Researchers need more data to "really get a better sense, beyond the leaf scale, how these ecosystems are responding to heat and drought," she added.

Recent research challenges a long-standing idea about how the brain develops: Rather than arising from a single source, the brain may emerge from two distinct populations of cells, the study finds.

"The brain appears as one organ," said study co-author Kyle Loh, an associate professor of developmental biology at Stanford University. "However, we discovered that the front part of the brain and the back part of the brain come from different sources, which are pushed together to create the appearance of a single organ," Loh told Live Science in an email.

The findings, published in September in the journal Nature Neuroscience, not only challenge established models of how the brain forms but may also explain why researchers have struggled to grow certain types of brain cells in the laboratory. The scientists say the work could offer new ways to investigate diseases that affect the brainstem, the "stalk" that connects the brain to the spinal cord.
The human brain is divided into three main regions — called the forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain — that perform different but interconnected functions.

The forebrain, which includes the cerebral hemispheres, is involved in higher-level cognitive processes, such as language, planning and abstract thinking. The midbrain, the uppermost part of the brainstem, connects the forebrain and the hindbrain and acts as a key relay center for sensory information and movement control. The hindbrain — which includes the bottom of the brainstem, along with other structures — also helps to coordinate movement, as well as regulate essential functions such as breathing, sleep and heart rate.
Historically, the hindbrain has been difficult to study. One reason is that scientists have faced persistent challenges in generating functional hindbrain neurons in laboratory conditions.

To help understand why, Loh and his team looked at the early stages of embryonic development in lab mice. They focused on gastrulation, the point when cells begin to organize into structures that will later form different organs. The researchers identified two distinct populations of immature cells that would go on to give rise to nervous system tissue, including the brain.

One cell population expressed a gene called Otx2, which helps to direct the early development of the forebrain and midbrain. The second group of cells expressed the gene Gbx2, which is involved in the development of the midbrain and hindbrain.

The functions of these genes were already known, but their distinct expression in these two groups of cells was revealed by the new research. The cell populations remained distinct as they developed into full-fledged nervous tissue, rather than overlapping.

The team also examined chromatin, the molecular structure that packages DNA tightly inside the nucleus and helps regulate which genes a cell can use. The two cell populations show different chromatin configurations, the team found, which further supports the idea that they follow separate developmental pathways.
That may help to explain why scientists' attempts to grow hindbrain neurons have been largely unsuccessful.

"Previous attempts to make hindbrain neurons likely tried to coax forebrain and midbrain progenitors into hindbrain cells, which our study shows is not possible," study co-author Rayyan Jokhai, a graduate student in Loh's lab, said in a statement.

Using the information uncovered in their experiments, the researchers successfully guided human stem cells to transform into functional hindbrain motor neurons, which are involved in controlling movement. Specifically, these cells produced proteins characteristic of the hard-to-grow hindbrain regions that help control muscles of the face and those involved in swallowing.

In several neurological diseases, including spinal muscular atrophy and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, motor neurons deteriorate and affected patients can lose their ability to swallow, speak and breathe independently.

"We cannot sample living motor neurons from a patient's hindbrain to watch how these diseases attack these neurons," Loh said. "Growing these hindbrain motor neurons in a dish gives us a way to investigate these diseases." Looking forward, the team aims to use their findings to study these diseases and pinpoint new treatments.
The new findings could also reveal something fundamental about the evolution of vertebrate animals.

The study authors investigated whether the two developmental pathways were unique to humans or reflected a much older evolutionary arrangement. They turned to previously published data on other species — including macaques (Macaca), zebrafish (Danio rerio) and chickens (Gallus gallus domesticus) — and again found two distinct cell populations expressing the two key genes.
And even in acorn worms — a marine invertebrate whose evolution diverged from vertebrates about 550 million years ago — they again found these two distinct groups of cells.

"The Stanford discovery establishes that the deep ancestry of the vertebrate brain is fundamentally modular," said Anna Di Cosmo, a professor of biology at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy who wasn't involved with the study. "The developmental separation between the anterior lineage (forebrain/midbrain) and the posterior lineage (hindbrain) is traceably ancient," Cosmo told Live Science in an email.

Loh's team speculates that these developmental trajectories seen in the womb may suggest that the two cell populations once belonged to two separate nervous systems. "Later in evolution, these two nervous systems may have been pushed together to give rise to the appearance of one integrated brain," Loh said.

However, the study doesn't reveal exactly when the two pathways arose or establish how they integrated. "It is important to emphasize that this is only an idea, and it might change as scientists learn more," Loh said.

A new 4,300-mile (7,000-kilometer) undersea fiber cable will shuttle data between the U.S. and France at breakneck speeds of up to 1 million gigabits per second (Gbps) — enough to move around 125 terabytes of data every second, or roughly 25,000 HD movies, each 5 gigabytes large. The cable, called Petal, will be funded and operated by Facebook and Instagram parent company Meta.

When it comes online in 2029, the ocean-spanning cable will be the first to deliver petabit capacity — double the capacity of existing subsea cables of this length — across transoceanic distances, Meta representatives said in a statement. That's enough to allow 75% of the world's population to stream music at once.

Petal will also be the first commercial subsea cable system to use multi-core fiber technology, according to the statement. Whereas conventional fiber strands typically contain a single core, each of Petal's fiber strands will contain two cores that carry optical signals in opposite directions, allowing a single strand to provide the capacity that would conventionally require a pair of single-core fibers.

Each fiber strand is roughly as thick as a human hair, measuring just 125 micrometers in diameter. Petal will contain 24 pairs of dual-core fibers, giving it 96 individual fiber cores in total and enabling it to carry as much data as 48 conventional fiber pairs, Meta engineers said.
Japanese technology company NEC will be responsible for the overall design and construction of Petal, while Sumitomo Electric will provide the fiber itself.

"Achieving petabit-per-second capacity across a transoceanic submarine system represents a major technological milestone in the history of global telecommunications," Eduardo Mateo, chief strategy officer of the Submarine Networks Division at NEC, said in the statement.

Subsea cables are among the most critical layers of internet infrastructure, carrying around 99% of the world's internet traffic, according to the International Telecommunication Union, the United Nations agency for digital technologies.

Installing thousands of miles of fragile glass cable on the ocean floor is an engineering feat in itself. Equally challenging is ensuring that these cables can carry the tiny pulses of infrared light that transport fiber-optic data across such huge distances without impacting performance.
This is typically achieved through repeaters — amplifiers installed at regular intervals along the cable that use lasers to boost the optical signals.
A 4,300-mile subsea cable typically needs about 100 of these repeaters to amplify the signals along its length, Meta representatives said.

Petal will incorporate something called "fan-in/fan-out" technology. As each two-core fiber strand enters a repeater, an optical interface routes the signal from each core into a separate single-core fiber strand so that each can be amplified independently. The amplified signals are then routed back into the two cores of the dual-core fiber before continuing along the cable.

Combined with its dual-core fiber, this feat of signal engineering will enable Petal to double its data-carrying capacity without requiring a proportional increase in power, Meta representatives said.

Petal is one of many subsea cable investments by Meta in recent years, including Marea in 2018, Amitie in 2023 and Anjana in 2025. Marea, the company's first transatlantic fiber instalment, supports 192 Tbps, meaning Petal will offer more than five times that capacity.
